DataConfig.java registers exactly two UserManager beans by design, @Bean(name = "online", isGeneric = true) and @Bean(name = "offline", isGeneric = true), and every other consumer in the codebase (e.g. IdentityContractConfig.userLookupContract) correctly takes @Qualifier("online") UserManager<Player>. Add @Qualifier("online") to the parameter on all 4 GangConfig methods (online is clearly correct for all four -- placeholders/options/debug/menus all concern currently-online players/targets, matching the existing pattern everywhere else). Add a red-first GangConfigBeanGraphTest case (the class already exists per fcc41a32) driving the real BeanFactory against GangConfig with both online/offline UserManager beans registered and asserting it does not throw.
location: gangland-features/gangland-gang/src/main/java/org/luckyraven/gangland/gang/GangConfig.java:125 (gangPlaceholderContribution), :135 (gangOptionContribution), :146 (gangDebugContribution), :174 (gangItemSourceContribution) -- all missing @Qualifier; gangland-impl/src/main/java/org/luckyraven/gangland/config/DataConfig.java:65-84 (the two isGeneric=true UserManager beans, "online"/"offline")
observation: Observed 2026-09-23 09:01 on the test server (0.10.0 @ fcc41a32, the T-53/T-54 fix commit) while re-running the 8-module smoke that T-53 previously blocked entirely: with T-53 fixed, boot now proceeds further and hits a NEW crash -- Gangland.onEnable throws java.lang.IllegalStateException: Ambiguous bean for parameter 'arg0' of type UserManager for bean GangConfig.gangItemSourceContribution(): 2 candidates registered. Add @Qualifier to disambiguate, at BeanFactory.resolveParameter <- invokeBean <- instantiate <- GanglandContext.bootstrap <- Gangland.onEnable. Plugin disables immediately, same downstream symptom as T-53 (every /glw subcommand throws unexpected error, command tree never registered). 100% reproducible across 2 separate boots this session (identical stack trace both times). A parallel 7-module run with the gang module entirely absent (so GangConfig never loads at all) had zero errors, confirming this is specific to GangConfig's own beans, not a wider regression. This was masked by T-53 in the previous merge round -- the plugin never reached CONFIG-phase bean instantiation far enough to hit it before this fix.

title: Duplicate default @Bean names silently overwrite each other in namedInstances and BeanGraph.byName
fix: Detect a duplicate BeanDefinition name at registration and fail fast (or namespace the default name by declaring @Configuration class)
observation: A @Bean method's default name is just the method name: `String name = beanAnnotation.name().isEmpty() ? method.getName() : beanAnnotation.name();` (BeanFactory.java:409). Two @Configuration classes each declaring a same-named method (e.g. two `settings()` beans in a consumer with many configuration classes) therefore produce the same name, and both registration sites overwrite blindly with no check or warning: `namedInstances.put(name, instance);` here, and `byName.put(def.name(), def);` at BeanGraph.java:39. A later @Qualifier("settings") injection then silently receives whichever bean was registered last, and BeanGraph.resolveProducer draws its dependency edge from `return byName.get(req.qualifier());` (BeanGraph.java:87) without ever comparing req.type(), so the graph edge can point at a bean of an entirely different type. Nothing logs the collision, so a consumer gets a wrong-but-plausible object injected with no diagnostic at boot.

title: ListenerService.registerGuarded falls back to registerEvents after per-method registration already partly succeeded
fix: Track the methods already registered and unregister them (or register into a staging list and commit only on success) before falling back
tests: ListenerServiceGuardTest (covers only a listener whose very first registerEvent throws, not a partially-registered multi-handler class)
observation: registerGuarded loops the listener's methods calling `pluginManager.registerEvent(eventType, listener, handler.priority(), executor, plugin, handler.ignoreCancelled());` one at a time, wrapped in a single try. The catch is `catch (Throwable t)` and its recovery is `pluginManager.registerEvents(listener, plugin);` which registers every @EventHandler in the class again. If the loop throws part-way — Bukkit's registerEvent raises IllegalPluginAccessException for an event class with no static getHandlerList, so handler #3 failing after #1 and #2 succeeded is a concrete trigger — the earlier handlers end up registered twice and every matching event runs them twice. In a consumer that is duplicated gameplay effect on one event (double payout, double item grant), which is why this is filed above P2.

title: classConditionsMet/methodConditionsMet run during configuration discovery, before any phase creates a bean
fix: Re-evaluate @ConditionalOnBean lazily at the point the owning phase instantiates the bean, not during the up-front discovery sweep
observation: The discovery loop evaluates `if (!classConditionsMet(configClass))` and `if (!methodConditionsMet(method))` while walking configuration classes, and only after that entire loop finishes does `for (Phase phase : Phase.values())` begin actually creating beans. A @ConditionalOnBean that names a bean produced by an earlier phase (say a CONFIG bean gating a LISTENER bean) is therefore always evaluated against a container that does not hold it yet, so the condition never passes and the bean is silently skipped with only a debug line. Only instances registered before instantiate() runs can satisfy the condition, which is not what the annotation's name implies and is not documented.

title: DependencyContainer stores each type's instances in a plain ArrayList inside a ConcurrentHashMap
fix: Use CopyOnWriteArrayList (or synchronize addUnique and the read paths) for the per-type instance lists
observation: The outer map is concurrent — `private final Map<Class<?>, List<Object>> instances = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();` — but the List values it holds are plain ArrayLists, giving the appearance of thread safety without it. A managed reload re-registers beans on the main thread while an async task started by a consumer resolves a dependency out of the same list, so a structural modification can race a read and yield a torn read or ConcurrentModificationException. No test exercises concurrent access, and the trigger requires a reload overlapping an async resolve, so this is filed as a latent trap rather than a proven live fault.

title: @AutowireTarget is a public shipped annotation with no consumers anywhere in the reactor
fix: Delete the annotation, or wire it into DependencyContainer.createInstance if constructor selection was the intent
observation: AutowireTarget is declared and exported as public API but nothing in keystone-bean or any sibling module reads it reflectively — a repo-wide grep finds only the declaration and its import. It reads as a constructor-selection marker a consumer would reasonably expect to work, so it is a dead feature that looks shipped rather than merely unused private code.

title: PostConstruct javadoc promises cross-@Configuration topological ordering the implementation does not provide
fix: Correct the javadoc to state that @PostConstruct order follows scan order across configuration classes
observation: The annotation's javadoc tells the reader that @PostConstruct callbacks run in topological order across configuration classes. BeanGraph.topologicalSort is applied per phase to that phase's BeanDefinitions, and the configuration classes themselves are walked in raw scan order, so the promised guarantee does not hold between two configuration classes in the same phase. This is documentation drift, not a behaviour bug, but a consumer relying on the stated ordering would write code that works by accident.

title: shutdownLifecycleBeans/reloadLifecycleBeans abort the whole pass when one bean throws
fix: Wrap each onShutdown/onPreClear/onClear/onInitialize/onPostInitialize call in a per-bean try/catch that reports through Diagnostics and continues
tests: BeanFactoryTest (shutdown/reload ordering only; no throwing-bean case)
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] Shutdown is a bare loop, `for (BeanLifecycle bean : reversed) { bean.onShutdown(); }`, and reloadLifecycleBeans (lines 333-353) runs three bare loops plus runPostInitialize the same way. BeanLifecycle documents onShutdown as the place to `flush pending state` and the order is reverse topological, so the beans that run last are the dependencies (repositories, data managers). A dependent whose onShutdown throws, for example touching a Bukkit API that is already unavailable during disable, skips every remaining bean's shutdown and loses their unflushed data. On reload, a throw in one onPreClear/onClear leaves some beans cleared and none re-initialized, so the plugin keeps running with empty state until restart. Neither path reports through Diagnostics, so the admin sees only a raw stack trace.

title: BeanGraph draws no edge for two same-phase producers of one type, hiding ambiguity
fix: When more than one same-phase definition can satisfy an unqualified requirement, add an edge from every candidate (or fail fast as ambiguous at graph-build time)
tests: BeanFactoryTest.unqualifiedParameterWithTwoCandidates_failsWithAmbiguousBean (producers in KERNEL, consumer in a later phase only)
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] resolveProducer returns an edge only for a single exact match (`if (exact != null && exact.size() == 1) return exact.get(0);`) and returns null as soon as a second assignable candidate appears (`if (assignable != null) return null;`), on the assumption stated in its comment that BeanFactory will flag the ambiguity at invocation. BeanFactory.resolveParameter (lines 514-531) only sees what is already registered, though, and with no edge the consumer's position in Kahn's order is simply its discovery position (config scan order plus getDeclaredMethods order, neither specified). If the consumer happens to run before both producers the bootstrap fails with a misleading `no bean of that type is registered`. If it runs between them it silently receives the first one and the ambiguity is never reported. The existing test passes only because its duplicates live in an earlier phase.

title: DependencyContainer ignores an unmatched @Qualifier and picks the first candidate
fix: Fail with a clear error when a @Qualifier name is not registered and when a type has more than one distinct instance, matching BeanFactory.resolveParameter
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] resolveConstructorParameters tries `instance = getInstance(qualifierName, paramType);` and, when that is null, falls straight back to `instance = getInstance(paramType);`, which returns `list.get(0)` whatever the list size (lines 56-62). Every @ListenerHandler, @CommandHandler and @Configuration instance is built through this path, so a constructor parameter annotated `@Qualifier("primary")` with a misspelled or unregistered name, or an unqualified parameter whose type has two beans, gets whichever instance registered first instead of failing. The @Bean-method path (BeanFactory.resolveParameter) rejects both cases (`no bean named '...'` / `Ambiguous bean`), so the same wiring mistake fails fast in one place and injects the wrong object in the other.

title: ListenerService.registerGuarded skips non-public @EventHandler methods, no setAccessible
fix: Collect getMethods() plus getDeclaredMethods() like JavaPluginLoader.createRegisteredListeners and call method.setAccessible(true) before registering
tests: ListenerServiceGuardTest (fixtures use only public handlers on public classes)
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] The guarded path reflects with `ReflectionGuard.<Method[]>orSkip(listenerClass, null, listenerClass::getMethods)`, so private, protected and package-private @EventHandler methods are never registered. Bukkit's own registerEvents, which this path replaces, unions getMethods() with getDeclaredMethods() and calls setAccessible(true). invokeHandler then does a plain `method.invoke(listener, event)` with no setAccessible, so a public handler declared on a non-public listener class throws IllegalAccessException from Keystone's package on every event; the Guard catches and reports it each time and the handler never runs. Neither case reaches the registerEvents fallback because registration itself succeeds. A consumer writing the ordinary Bukkit idiom `@EventHandler void onJoin(PlayerJoinEvent e)` gets a listener that silently does nothing. Current consumer listeners all use public handlers on public classes, so this is a latent trap rather than a live outage.

title: CommandManager.onHelp renders a subcommand's help without the permission check runExecute enforces
fix: Check sender.hasPermission(command.getPermission()) in onHelp before calling help(), as onHelpAll already does via permissibleCommands
observation: The dispatch loop picks between execution and help with `if (Arrays.stream(args).anyMatch("help"::equalsIgnoreCase)) onHelp(entry, sender, args); else entry.getValue().runExecute(label, sender, args);`. runExecute opens with `if (!sender.hasPermission(permission)) { sender.sendMessage(CommandMessages.noPermission()); return; }` (Command.java:78-81) but onHelp goes straight to `entry.getValue().help(sender, page);` with no check at all. Any player can therefore type `/<label> <restricted-subcommand> help` and read the full syntax and description of a command they cannot run. The sibling path onHelpAll deliberately iterates `permissibleCommands(sender)`, so permission-filtered help is clearly the intent and this branch is the hole; filed P1 rather than P0 because it discloses command structure but executes nothing.

title: Argument.execute coerces any token merely containing the substring confirm into the literal confirm token
fix: Match the token exactly (equalsIgnoreCase("confirm")) instead of contains, when wrapping input args
observation: Every user token is wrapped with `if (arg.toLowerCase().contains("confirm")) return new ConfirmArgument(plugin, tree); return new Argument(plugin, arg, tree);`, and ConfirmArgument's constructor calls `super(plugin, "confirm", tree, action)` so its arguments array is exactly {"confirm"}. Any free-text value containing the substring — a mail body word like "confirmed", a gang name "Confirmation" — is therefore rewritten to the literal token "confirm" before tree matching, so it stops matching the OptionalArgument node it belongs to and instead matches a confirm branch. The destructive-action gate itself still holds, because the lock test lives on the registered tree node's ConfirmArgument.executeArgument (`if (!lock.isLocked(sender))`), not on this input wrapper — so this is input corruption, not a confirm bypass.

title: BrigadierPaperListener.handle swallows ReflectiveOperationException, leaving the unfiltered permission-leaking tree in place
fix: Report the reflective failure through Diagnostics (once) instead of an empty catch, so the degraded state is visible
observation: The entire per-event body is wrapped in `catch (ReflectiveOperationException ignored) { // No realistic recovery — the unfiltered tree (if any) stays in place. }` with no log and no Diagnostics report. This class exists specifically to remove PaperCommodore's unfiltered shared command node and replace it with a per-player permission-filtered tree, so when the reflection fails the fallback state is exactly the leak it was written to prevent: every player's client sees completions for commands they cannot run. Because the catch is silent, an admin gets no signal that command-completion filtering has stopped working on their server build.

title: ArgumentLock never releases a sender who disconnects mid-confirmation, retaining the Player strongly
fix: Remove the sender on PlayerQuitEvent, or key the set on UUID with a timeout instead of holding CommandSender
observation: The lock set is `private final Set<CommandSender> lockedSenders = new HashSet<>();` populated by lock() and emptied only by unlock(), which fires solely from ConfirmArgument.executeArgument on a successful second invocation. A player who triggers the first half of a confirm gate and then logs out is never removed, so the set retains a strong reference to a Player object — and through it the entity and its world references — for the remaining uptime of the server. Every abandoned confirmation adds another, so this grows monotonically on a busy server. There is no correctness impact on rejoin (the returning player is a new CommandSender and correctly unlocked), making this purely an uptime leak.

title: Argument.traverseList returns NO_PERMISSION from the first child instead of trying the remaining siblings
fix: Record the NO_PERMISSION result and keep scanning siblings, returning it only if no sibling succeeds
tests: ArgumentTreeTest (constructs NO_PERMISSION but not the sibling-fallthrough case)
observation: The sibling loop is `if (result.getState() == ResultState.SUCCESS) return result; else if (result.getState() == ResultState.NO_PERMISSION) return ArgumentResult.noPermission(node.getData());` — the first child that denies permission ends the whole search. Where two sibling nodes can match the same token (a permission-gated literal alongside an ungated OptionalArgument wildcard, which is a normal shape in this framework), a player who legitimately matches the second branch is told they lack permission instead of running it. Requires that specific overlapping-sibling tree shape, hence P2.

title: BrigadierPaperListener gates the tree on PluginCommand#getPermission() rather than the permission CommandManager enforces
fix: Gate on the same permission string CommandManager checks, not the plugin.yml PluginCommand permission
observation: The master gate is `String masterPerm = command.getPermission(); if (masterPerm != null && !masterPerm.isEmpty() && !player.hasPermission(masterPerm)) return;`, reading Bukkit's plugin.yml-declared PluginCommand permission — a different string from the one CommandManager actually enforces at dispatch. When plugin.yml declares no permission the gate is skipped entirely; when it declares a different one the wrong check runs. Per-argument predicates still filter individual nodes, so the consequence is a mismatch between what the client tree shows at the root and what dispatch enforces rather than an outright bypass.

title: BrigadierTabRegistrar permission and visibility predicates return true when extractSender cannot resolve the Bukkit sender
fix: Fail closed (return false) when the sender cannot be extracted from the NMS source
observation: permissionRequires builds `source -> { CommandSender sender = extractSender(source); if (sender == null) return true; return sender.hasPermission(permission); }`, and visibilityRequires does the same. extractSender resolves the Bukkit sender reflectively from the NMS command source, so on any server build where that reflection does not match, every permission predicate answers true and the client is offered completions for commands the player cannot run. The failure is silent and version-dependent, and it fails open rather than closed on a permission decision.

title: CommandManager's static defaultInstance shares per-plugin command state across every consumer on the shared classloader
fix: Remove the static accessors (already deprecated) so each consumer resolves its own CommandManager instance
observation: `private static volatile CommandManager defaultInstance;` is claimed by whichever CommandManager is constructed first in the JVM, and the static getCommands/getPermissibleCommands accessors delegate to it. Keystone is loaded once and shared by Gangland, Bartizan and Oriel, so on a server running two consumers the second plugin's static lookups return the first plugin's command registry — exactly the per-plugin static state the repo's shared-classloader rule forbids. The field's own javadoc concedes the accessors "go away in 2.0.0", so it is a known deprecated hazard rather than an unnoticed one.

title: CommandMessages and ArgumentMessages hold their overrides in static fields, so one consumer's install() rewrites every plugin's command text
fix: Move the override state onto the CommandManager instance so each consumer owns its own strings
observation: Every message supplier is static — `private static Supplier<String> noPermission = DEFAULT_NO_PERMISSION;` and six siblings, with the same pattern in ArgumentMessages — and install() replaces them process-wide. With Keystone shared across consumers, whichever plugin calls install() last owns the framework's player-facing strings for all of them, so a Gangland player can be shown Oriel's localized no-permission text. The javadoc documents this as "one consumer plugin owns the command framework's strings", but it still contradicts the hard shared-classloader rule and produces visibly wrong output on a multi-consumer server.

title: CommandManager.onCommand treats an exact help token anywhere in args as a help request
fix: Only treat help as a help request in the position immediately after the subcommand
observation: The check is `Arrays.stream(args).anyMatch("help"::equalsIgnoreCase)`, scanning every typed token rather than the position after the subcommand. Any command carrying free text where a value can legitimately be the word "help" — a mail message, a search term, a player-supplied name — is silently diverted into onHelp and the intended action never runs. The user sees a help page instead of their command executing, with no indication why.

title: TargetSelector.origin overrides the selection world without recomputing the origin coordinates in that world
fix: Recompute originX/Y/Z relative to the named world (its spawn) when a world= filter replaces the sender's world
tests: TargetSelectorTest (no cross-world world= plus distance/sort case)
observation: origin() first derives originX/Y/Z from the sender's own location (or the default world's spawn), and only afterwards applies the explicit world filter with `if (this.world != null) { World named = Bukkit.getWorld(this.world); if (named == null) return null; world = named; }`, swapping the World reference while leaving the coordinates from the previous world in place. A selector combining a world filter with a distance or nearest-sort then measures distances from a point that does not correspond to anything in the target world, so the wrong entities are selected or ordered. Only affects selectors that cross worlds, hence P2.

title: Argument.addSubArgument picks tree-insertion order by substring-matching "?" in the token text instead of checking the type
fix: Test `argument instanceof OptionalArgument` rather than searching the token for the "?" character
observation: Insertion order is chosen by `if (argument.toString().contains(OPTIONAL_ARGUMENT)) node.add(argument.getNode()); else node.add(0, argument.getNode());`, where toString() returns the literal token and OPTIONAL_ARGUMENT is the single character "?". A plain literal sub-argument whose own token happens to contain a question mark is appended last like a wildcard instead of prepended, changing which sibling wins during matching. The trigger requires a literal token containing "?", which is unusual, so this is a latent correctness trap rather than an observed fault.

title: Argument.notFound reports the last valid token as the invalid one when the args end on a valid node
fix: Distinguish "ended on a valid node" from "next token invalid" and word the message accordingly
observation: When the matched token is also the final element of args, the else branch keeps `length = i` and sets `lastInput = args[length]`, which is the token that just matched successfully. The error message therefore names a valid token as the invalid input, telling a user that the very argument they typed correctly is wrong. Purely a message-accuracy defect on an already-failing path.

title: Argument overrides equals() by content but never overrides hashCode()
fix: Add a matching hashCode(), or drop the equals override if identity comparison is what the tree needs
observation: equals() compares the two arguments arrays case-insensitively with anyMatch, so two distinct Argument objects sharing one alias are equal, yet no hashCode() override accompanies it and Object identity hashing remains. Equal instances therefore hash differently, which silently breaks any HashSet or HashMap keyed on Argument. Nothing in the reactor currently hashes an Argument — the tree stores children in lists — so this is a contract violation waiting for the first hashed use rather than a live fault.

title: Free-text argument nodes on the Paper Brigadier path carry no suggestion provider, so tab completion never asks the server
fix: Attach a suggestion provider (ASK_SERVER: (ctx, builder) -> builder.buildFuture()) to every free-text string node BrigadierTabRegistrar builds (OptionalArgument and the ListArgument fallback) on both backends, so the client round-trips to CommandTabCompleter and OptionalArgument suppliers become reachable
tests: BrigadierTabRegistrarTest (asserts every ArgumentCommandNode of a give <name> <amount> tree has non-null getCustomSuggestions())
observation: FIXED Keystone 1.9.2, branch phase-h9-host-api (uncommitted 2026-09-13, docs/phase-h9-host-api.md section 6; found and fixed by the Bartizan session while diagnosing /bartizan weapon give <tab> on Paper 1.21.11). BrigadierTabRegistrar mapped every OptionalArgument and the ListArgument fallback to a plain string() node with no suggestion provider; the client tree serialiser marks a node ask-the-server only when a provider is present, so on the Paper path (BrigadierPaperListener ships the tree as built) the client never asked CommandTabCompleter and every live OptionalArgument supplier (player names, module ids, waypoint names) was unreachable. Spigot was unaffected only because Commodore installs its own dummy provider.

title: CommandTabCompleter.descend skips permission checks on intermediate argument nodes
fix: Check each matched node's permission in descend/findArgument (as Argument.traverseList does) and return no suggestions below a node the sender lacks
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] descend matches each child purely on its token (`if (!argumentMatches(child.getData(), args[currentIndex], children)) continue; if (currentIndex == targetDepth) return child.getData();`) and never consults the matched node's getPermission(); the only permission filter is on the final children list (`if (permission.isEmpty() || sender.hasPermission(permission)) suggestions.addAll(...)`, lines 103-108). Sub-arguments default to an empty permission (Argument.java:50), so for a tree `/cmd gang admin <player>` where only `admin` is gated, a player without that permission who types `/cmd gang admin <tab>` receives admin's children, including OptionalArgument customStrings (player/gang name lists). Dispatch rejects the same path at the gated node (Argument.traverseList returns NO_PERMISSION), so completion and execution disagree. The Brigadier trees filter per node, but this server-side completer is what answers on the fallback path (Commodore unsupported or registration failed) and for any tab-complete request a client sends for the gated prefix.

title: Argument.notFound suggests permission-gated sub-argument names in its did-you-mean line
fix: Filter the did-you-mean dictionary to children whose permission is empty or held by the sender, as CommandManager.onCommand already does via permissibleCommands
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] On a NOT_FOUND result the suggestion dictionary is every child of the last valid node: `Set<String> dictionary = children.stream().map(node -> node.getData().arguments).flatMap(Stream::of).filter(s -> !s.equals(OPTIONAL_ARGUMENT)).collect(Collectors.toSet());` with no permission check, and the closest match is sent back via `ArgumentMessages.didYouMean(suggestion)`. A player who mistypes near a gated literal under a parent they can reach (e.g. `/cmd sub resett` where the child `reset` carries a permission they lack) is told the exact name of a sub-argument they are not permitted to see. The master-level suggestion in CommandManager.onCommand builds its dictionary from `permissibleCommands(sender)`, so filtering is clearly the intent and this branch is the hole; disclosure only, nothing executes.

title: BrigadierPaperListener.handle drops master-command alias nodes and never re-adds them
fix: After building the per-player tree, also add a renamed copy (redirect or rebuilt literal) under each of command.getAliases(), as Commodore does
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] The handler strips the Bukkit stub for the name and every alias (`removeChild(root, command.getName()); for (String alias : command.getAliases()) removeChild(root, alias);`) and then adds exactly one node, `root.addChild(tree)`, whose literal is `LiteralArgumentBuilder.literal(command.getName())` (BrigadierTabRegistrar.java:153). On the Paper backend (servers that still fire AsyncPlayerSendCommandsEvent) every master-command alias from plugin.yml therefore disappears from the client's command tree: typing `/<alias> ` renders as an unknown command with no suggestions at all, not even the server-side CommandTabCompleter stub that was there before the listener removed it. The Spigot backend does not have this gap because Commodore registers the node under every alias. Execution is unaffected (Bukkit dispatch still resolves the alias), so this is a missing-UX defect.

title: BrigadierTabRegistrar emits only arguments[0], so subcommand aliases vanish client-side
fix: Emit one literal (or a redirect to the canonical node) per entry in Command.getAlias() and per extra token in Argument.getArguments() on both backends
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] Subcommand nodes are built as `LiteralArgumentBuilder.literal(cmd.getLabel())` (lines 163 and 227) and plain sub-arguments as `LiteralArgumentBuilder.literal(arg.getArguments()[0])` (lines 359 and 380); Command.getAlias() and the remaining Argument tokens are never emitted. CommandManager.onCommand dispatches aliases (`entry.getValue().getAlias().contains(args[0].toLowerCase())`) and CommandTabCompleter.resolve completes them, but once the Brigadier tree is shipped the client parses locally, so `/cmd <sub-alias> ...` shows as an incorrect argument in red and nothing below it completes, on both the Paper and Spigot backends. Any consumer that gives a subcommand a short alias (the Command constructor's `String... alias`) hits this on every use; the command still runs when sent.

title: DoubleArgument/ConfirmArgument stay armed forever: ArgumentLock arms never expire
fix: Store an arm timestamp per sender in ArgumentLock and treat arms older than a short window (e.g. 30s) as unlocked; clear stale arms on the next lock check
tests: DoubleArgumentTest, ConfirmArgumentTest (neither covers a delayed second invocation)
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] DoubleArgument's safety gate is `if (!lock.isLocked(sender)) { sender.sendMessage(ArgumentMessages.confirmPrompt()); lock.lock(sender); return; } lock.unlock(sender); super.executeArgument(sender, args);`, and ArgumentLock (ArgumentLock.java:12-28) is a bare `Set<CommandSender>` with no time or context attached. A player who runs a type-it-twice destructive command once, reads the prompt and backs out, then runs it again an hour later expecting the prompt gets immediate execution instead; ConfirmArgument has the same shape, so `/<cmd> confirm` completes a confirmation armed at any earlier point in the session (Gangland's gang transfer flow arms `confirmTransfer.lock(sender)` and relies on this gate). Distinct from KS-CM-04, which files the same set's memory retention on disconnect; this row is the correctness side, a confirmation gate that never lapses.

title: CommandManager.clearCommands advises a re-scan that CommandService silently skips
fix: Clear CommandService.scannedPackages in clearCommands (or add a resetScans() the javadoc points to) so the documented reload flow repopulates the registry
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] clearCommands is documented as `Removes every registered subcommand — call before a re-scan on reload.` and does `registry.clear()`, but the re-scan it points to, CommandService.scanAndRegisterCommands, opens with `if (!scannedPackages.add(basePackage)) { log.debug("Package {} already scanned for commands — skipping", basePackage); return; }` (keystone-bean CommandService.java:54-57) and nothing ever removes entries from scannedPackages. A consumer following the javadoc (clearCommands, then scanAndRegisterCommands with the same package, as Gangland/Oriel/Bartizan bootstraps call it) ends the reload with an empty registry: every subcommand answers as unknown until restart, and the only trace is a DEBUG line. No consumer calls clearCommands yet, so this is a documented reload path that cannot work rather than a live outage.

title: BrigadierTabRegistrar.paperListenerCommands is static per-plugin state keyed by name
fix: Key the dedup on the plugin (or keep it on the CommandManager instance) and drop the entry when the plugin disables
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] `private static final Set<String> paperListenerCommands = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();` gates registration with `if (!paperListenerCommands.add(command.getName())) { ...; return; }` (lines 186-190) and is never cleared. Keystone's classes outlive a single consumer, so when a consumer is disabled and re-enabled without Keystone reloading (PlugMan-style reload), Bukkit unregisters the old BrigadierPaperListener on disable but the re-enable skips registering a new one because the name is still in the set, leaving no per-player tree for that command. Two consumers whose master commands share a name likewise only get one listener. This is the per-plugin static state the shared-classloader rule forbids.

title: CommandManager.addCommand ignores label/alias collisions; dispatch and completion diverge
fix: Reject (or Diagnostics-report) a subcommand whose label or alias is already claimed in addCommand
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] addCommand is `registry.put(sub.getLabel(), sub);`, so a second subcommand with the same label silently replaces the first, and aliases are never compared against other labels. Dispatch walks the registry in insertion order and takes the first entry where `entry.getKey().equalsIgnoreCase(args[0]) || entry.getValue().getAlias().contains(args[0].toLowerCase())` (lines 195-197), while CommandTabCompleter.resolve checks every label before any alias (CommandTabCompleter.java:116-127). If subcommand A, scanned first, declares alias `b` and subcommand B has label `b`, then `/cmd b ...` executes A while tab completion walks B's argument tree, and nothing warns the author. Needs an authoring mistake to trigger, hence P3.

title: Argument.notFound blames the free-text token after an OptionalArgument, not the typo
fix: Walk the tree for the last valid node with the same OptionalArgument wildcard matching traverseList uses, so free-text positions count as valid
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] notFound finds the last valid node with `tree.traverseLastValid(modifiedArg)`, but Tree.traverseLastValid only matches by `node.getData().equals(list[index])` (keystone-common Tree.java:122-131) with no wildcard, and an OptionalArgument's tokens are just `?`, so the walk always stops at the literal before the first free-text position. For `/cmd set Steve of` on a tree set -> <name> -> {on, off}, the loop finds `set` and reports `lastInput = args[length]`, the valid name `Steve`, as the wrong argument, and the typo `of` is never mentioned; the did-you-mean line is built from set's children, which after the `?` filter is empty. This hits any typo after a free-text argument. Distinct from KS-CM-13, which covers args that end on a valid node.

title: ItemConverterRegistry.resolve gates the MATERIAL converter on raw Material.valueOf instead of XMaterial
fix: Resolve through XMaterial.matchXMaterial(type) so cross-version material aliases still reach the MATERIAL converter
observation: resolve() decides whether an unknown type string is a material by attempting `Material.valueOf(type.toUpperCase());` and treating IllegalArgumentException as "not a material", returning null. Bukkit's Material constants drift across the 1.16.5-to-current span Keystone supports (GRASS_PATH became DIRT_PATH in 1.17, among others), so a config written against one server version fails this check on another and the item definition silently resolves to no converter at all. This is the only raw valueOf left in the module — ItemBuilder already resolves through `XMaterial.PLAYER_HEAD.get()` at lines 200-218 — so it is both a version-drift bug and a violation of the repo's XSeries convention. The failure is silent: the caller just gets null.

title: ItemBuilder.decreaseDurability and setDurability never clamp damage against getItemMaxDurability()
fix: Clamp the computed damage into 0..getItemMaxDurability() inside setDurability
observation: decreaseDurability computes `return setDurability((short) (currentDurability + amount));` and setDurability applies it with `damageable.setDamage(durability);` — neither consults getItemMaxDurability(), which sits two methods away and knows the real limit. Repeated decreases, or one oversized amount from a consumer's config, push the stored damage past the material's maximum (and a negative amount pushes it below zero), producing a stack whose damage value is outside the range the client's durability bar can render. The item does not break at the boundary the way vanilla damage does, so a consumer implementing wear-and-tear gets an item stuck in an invalid damage state rather than a broken one.

title: ItemVocabularies.install leaves partial registrations behind when a vocabulary's contribute throws
fix: Buffer a vocabulary's registrations and commit to the shared registries only after contribute returns cleanly
observation: RegistrarImpl writes each converter/serializer/refresher straight into the shared live registries as the vocabulary calls it, and the failure path is `catch (Throwable t) { report(namespace, t); continue; }` — the calls that already landed are never rolled back. A vocabulary that registers several entries and then throws part-way leaves the item registries holding an arbitrary prefix of its contributions while the fault report tells the admin the vocabulary failed. The consumer then runs with a half-installed item vocabulary whose behaviour depends on where the exception happened, which is worse than either installing it or not.

title: ItemBuilder.setAmount and setItemMeta skip the null and bounds guards every sibling method applies
fix: Add the same `itemStack == null` guard the sibling methods use, and reject amounts outside 1..max stack size
observation: The class deliberately tolerates a null stack — the copy constructor does `source.itemStack == null ? null : source.itemStack.clone()` and withMeta, decreaseDurability, getItemMaxDurability, getItemDamagedDurability and setDurability all open with an `itemStack == null` guard. setAmount does not: `public ItemBuilder setAmount(int amount) { itemStack.setAmount(amount); return this; }` throws NPE on exactly the state its siblings handle, and setItemMeta at line 194 has the same gap. It also passes the amount through unvalidated, so a config-supplied `0` yields an empty stack rather than an error. Filed P3 because no caller in the reactor is known to hit either state today.

title: ReflectiveNbtApiAccessor.method caches only successful lookups, re-reflecting and warning on every miss
fix: Cache the negative result (a sentinel) so an unresolvable method warns once instead of on every call
observation: method() consults methodCache first but writes to it only on the found branch; the not-found path ends `log.warn("NBT provider does not expose {}({} args)", name, argCount); return null;` without recording the miss. If the bound NBTAPI build lacks one of the hardcoded accessor names, every subsequent item operation redoes the full reflective scan and emits another warn line, so a single incompatibility becomes repeated reflection cost plus console spam proportional to item throughput. Cosmetic and performance rather than correctness, hence P3.

title: ItemParser drops a second {...} attribute block instead of reporting it as malformed
fix: Report a user-error Fault when more than one attribute block is present rather than stripping it silently
observation: The parser reads attributes from the first block only — `if (matcher.find())` then `KEY_VALUE_PATTERN.matcher(matcher.group(1))` — but cleans up with `remaining = matcher.replaceAll("").trim();`, which strips every `{...}` occurrence in the string. A definition such as `tool{a=1}{b=2}` therefore parses as type `tool` with only `a=1`, and the admin gets no indication that the second block was discarded. The surrounding code does report other malformed shapes through Result.fail with a user-error Fault, so silence here is inconsistent with the file's own error handling.

title: ItemParser/ItemConverterRegistry case-fold with the default locale, breaking tr_TR hosts
fix: Use toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT)/toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT) at every registry and parser fold
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] ItemParser does `String type = parts[0].toUpperCase();`, and ItemConverterRegistry keys and looks up with `type.toLowerCase()` (L33, L69, L75) and checks materials with `Material.valueOf(type.toUpperCase())` (L94), all using the JVM default locale. Under tr_TR, `diamond_sword`.toUpperCase() is `DİAMOND_SWORD` (dotted capital I), so Material.valueOf rejects it and ItemParser returns item.unknown_type for every material whose name contains an i (diamond, iron, stick, ...), and consumer kinds like `item` stop matching their registered keys. ItemSerializerRegistry (L69) and MaterialItemSerializer (L30) fold the same way on the write side. Bukkit's own Material.matchMaterial uses Locale.ENGLISH for exactly this reason, and the rest of keystone-common (DurationParser, PdcPlayerMetaService) already passes Locale.ROOT.

title: ItemParser.tryParse lets a throwing converter escape instead of returning a Fault
fix: Wrap converter.convert in Guard/Result.of (and the same call in ItemDslAdapter) and map any throwable to CODE_CONVERSION_FAILED with the input attached
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] tryParse is documented as "reporting the cause of any failure as a USER_ERROR Fault", but it calls `ItemStack converted = converter.convert(viewer, type, modifier, attributes);` unguarded and only handles a null return. Converters are consumer-supplied and take user-authored modifier and attribute strings (for example `{custom_model_data=abc}`), so a converter that does Integer.parseInt on one propagates NumberFormatException out of a method whose return type is Result, and a config load iterating many items aborts on the first bad entry. ItemDslAdapter.java:120 makes the same unguarded `converter.convert(type, modifier, attrs)` call, so the config-DSL path with file:line reporting loses the location as well.

title: ItemBuilder.setMaxStackSize writes an ignored custom_data tag, so it never takes effect
fix: On 1.20.5+ call ItemMeta#setMaxStackSize(Integer) reflectively (resolve it once, like WorldHeights does for getMinHeight) instead of writing an NBT tag
tests: ItemBuilderMaxStackSizeTest (pins only that a tag write happens)
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] The method returns early below 1.20.5, and on 1.20.5+ it does `return addTag("max_stack_size", size);`, which goes through NbtBridge to NBT-API's NBT.modify(ItemStack, ...). On 1.20.5+ NBT.modify edits the item's minecraft:custom_data component, not the minecraft:max_stack_size data component, so the stack keeps its vanilla limit and the call has no effect on any server. The javadoc ("Sets the stack's maximum stack size") and the green test, which asserts only `assertEquals("max_stack_size", accessor.writes.get(0).tag())`, make the feature look shipped.

title: FileManager.runInitializer regenerates the live config from jar on any Exception, not just parse failures
fix: Only regenerate on parse/IO exceptions from the file itself; let unrelated initializer exceptions propagate or be logged without touching the file
observation: runInitializer wraps the whole consumer callback in `catch (Exception first)` with no filtering on exception type, then calls `handler.createNewFile()` on any failure. createNewFile moves the admin's live file aside — `Files.move(file.toPath(), oldFile.toPath(), StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);` (FileHandler.java:125) — and writes the jar default in its place, logging "is an old build or corrupted, creating a new one". So a bug anywhere inside a consumer's initialize() (an NPE reading an unrelated manager, a NumberFormatException on a value it computed) silently swaps the admin's tuned config for defaults on the next boot. The edited file survives as `<name>-old.yml` so this is recoverable rather than true data loss, which is why it is P1 and not P0; the server still comes up running default settings with only a warn line.

title: FileHandler.registerYamlFile swallows InvalidConfigurationException with no log at all
fix: Log the parse failure through logException/Diagnostics before setting loaded=false
observation: The YAML load is guarded by `catch (InvalidConfigurationException exception) { loaded = false; }` — no log call, unlike every sibling catch in the class which routes through logException/log.warn/log.error. An admin who leaves a tab character or a duplicate key in a config gets no message whatsoever; the handler simply reports not-loaded and every value silently falls back to defaults. The identical silent pattern repeats in createNewFile's post-regeneration reload at line 139, `catch (IOException | InvalidConfigurationException ignored) { loaded = false; }`. This is the archetypal admin-invisible failure the repo's own Result/Diagnostics rule exists to prevent.

title: ConfigSerializer.scalarToJava does not strip digit-grouping underscores, so 10_000_000 degrades to a String
fix: Run the value through the same normalizeNumeric helper NodeReader uses before parseLong/parseDouble
observation: NodeReader treats underscore digit grouping as a supported config convention — normalizeNumeric (NodeReader.java:55-67) strips `_` between digits so `10_000_000` parses, and the reader path uses it at line 231. ConfigSerializer's parallel path does not: the Tag.INT branch is `long parsed = Long.parseLong(value.trim());` and the Tag.FLOAT branch `return Double.parseDouble(value.trim());`, each with `catch (NumberFormatException e) { return value; }`. An underscore-grouped number therefore silently comes back as the String "10_000_000" instead of a number, so a consumer reading it as an int gets a type mismatch or its default, and a round trip through the serializer rewrites the value as a quoted string. Two supported spellings of the same config value behave differently depending on which reader path touches it.

title: ConfigParser.convert recurses without a cycle guard, so a self-referencing YAML anchor throws StackOverflowError
fix: Track visited snakeyaml nodes during convert and emit a ConfigIssue on a cycle instead of recursing
observation: The class javadoc promises the parser never throws on bad input, and parse() does catch `MarkedYAMLException`/`YAMLException` around `yaml.compose(reader)`. But convert/convertMapping/convertSequence then walk the composed node graph with plain recursion and no visited-set, so a recursive anchor such as `a: &x {b: *x}` — which snakeyaml composes into a genuinely cyclic node graph — recurses until StackOverflowError. That is an Error, not an Exception, so the parser's own guards do not catch it and it escapes to the caller, breaking the documented never-throws contract. Requires a hand-written recursive anchor, hence P2 rather than higher.

title: FolderLoader.loadData only regenerates expected files when the whole folder is empty
fix: Diff expectedFolderFiles against the folder contents in the else branch and create the missing ones
observation: expectedFolderFiles is consulted only inside `if (!folder.exists() || files == null || files.length == 0)`. The else branch is just `addFiles(files); if (folderFiles.isEmpty()) return;` and never checks whether each expected default is actually present. If an admin deletes one file out of a populated folder, or a new Keystone version adds an expected file to a folder that already has others, that file is never recreated and the feature depending on it is silently absent. Recovery only happens if the admin empties the entire folder.

title: FileLoader.tryAgain calls load() on every scheduled tick even after isLoaded flips true
fix: Return after time.stop() so a successful load is not reloaded by the remaining ticks
observation: The retry body is `if (isLoaded) time.stop(); load(disable, consumer, fileManager);` — stop() only cancels future ticks, so load() still runs once more on the tick that observed success, redundantly re-reading and re-consuming the file. No caller in the reactor invokes tryAgain, so the cost today is a latent trap in unused public API rather than observed behaviour, which is why it is P3.

title: NodeReader.asDouble accepts NaN and Infinity, which min() and max() range guards cannot reject
fix: Treat non-finite parse results as invalid in asDouble (report config.double and mark INVALID)
observation: asDouble parses with `return new DoubleAccess(Double.parseDouble(normalizeNumeric(scalar.value())), State.VALID, path, scalar.location(), report);`, and Double.parseDouble happily accepts the literals `NaN`, `Infinity` and `-Infinity`, marking them VALID. The range guards then cannot catch them, because every NaN comparison is false: `min` tests `if (state == State.VALID && value < min)` (line 492) so `NaN < 0` fails and the value passes, and `max`'s `value > max` fails identically — positive Infinity likewise slips through any lone `.min(0)`. The class javadoc's own worked example is `r.get("Sell_Price_Ratio").asDouble().min(0).required().orElse(1.0)`, so a config typo of `NaN` flows straight into price arithmetic where it silently poisons every derived value, since NaN propagates through arithmetic without ever throwing. Also Oriel OR-DI-03.

title: ConfigParser ignores YAML merge keys, so values inherited through <<: *anchor never reach NodeReader
fix: When a mapping key carries Tag.MERGE, flatten the referenced mapping(s) into the entries (explicit keys win), mirroring SnakeYAML's constructor
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] parse() builds the tree from `yaml.compose(reader)`, and SnakeYAML's composer only flags merge keys; the `<<` flattening happens in the constructor that Bukkit's YamlConfiguration uses. convertMapping copies node tuples verbatim (`String key = keyScalar.getValue(); ... entries.put(key, child);`), so `S: {<<: *b, C: 3}` becomes a mapping whose keys are literally `<<` and `C` (verified with snakeyaml 1.28: compose yields keys "<< C" while load yields {A=1, B=2, C=3}). Bukkit's getters on the same file see the merged keys, but a loader on NodeReader gets MISSING for every inherited key (silent default, or a config.required error) plus a spurious "unknown key '<<'" warning from the sweep. A config that loads correctly through FileConfiguration therefore loses values once its loader moves to the positional reader.

title: FileHandler(JavaPlugin, File) keeps only the immediate parent folder, so nested files regenerate against the wrong path
fix: Derive directory from the file's path relative to plugin.getDataFolder() instead of the last parent segment
tests: FolderLoaderRecursionTest (discovers nested files but never regenerates one); FileHandlerIntegrationTest.relativeParentName_handlesBothSeparators (pins separator handling only)
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] The File constructor sets `directory` from relativeParentName, which returns `parentPath.substring(sepIndex + 1)`, the last segment only. FolderLoader recurses into sub-folders (FolderLoader.java:132-137, pinned by FolderLoaderRecursionTest) and accepts nested folders such as "configs/menus", so a file at <data>/menus/imported/inner.yml gets directory "imported/inner". Every regeneration then computes paths from that wrong root: createNewFile moves the file to `new File(plugin.getDataFolder(), directory + "-old" + fileType)`, i.e. <data>/imported/inner-old.yml, whose parent usually does not exist, so the move fails and regeneration is skipped with a warn; when that folder does exist the move succeeds, the jar lookup on the wrong path misses, and the fallback `file.createNewFile()` leaves an empty file in place of the admin's. Triggered by a Config_Version mismatch in registerYamlFile, or by FileManager.reloadFiles recovery on a parse failure.

title: RepositoryRegistry.canRegisterRepository inverts its Table check, defeating ordering and logging a false circular dependency
fix: Swap the branches so a missing table returns false and a present table continues the loop
observation: The dependency check is backwards: `if (!tablesByName.containsKey(tableName)) { continue; }` skips the parameter when the table is absent, and then the code logs "depends on table {} which is not yet registered" and returns false for the case where the table IS present. sortRepositoriesByDependencies therefore refuses every repository whose Table dependency is already satisfied, makes no progress, and falls into its escape hatch at line 332 which logs "Circular dependency in repositories detected, registering remaining repositories in order" and appends the rest in declaration order. The net effect on every consumer boot is that table-dependency ordering is silently not applied, plus a misleading circular-dependency warning; FK-bearing schemas that need parent-before-child creation are then at the mercy of scan order.

title: DatabaseHelper caches getDatabase() at construction, so a helper built before connect() makes every runQueries a silent no-op
fix: Resolve the Database from the handler on each call instead of caching it in a final field
observation: The constructor snapshots the handler's current Database once: `this.database = databaseHandler.getDatabase();`. Every query path then uses that captured reference and opens with `if (database == null) return;` (line 47), so a helper constructed before the handler has resolved its database swallows every subsequent query silently — no exception, no log, no fault. The same staleness applies after the handler swaps its Database (the MySQL to SQLite fallback, or a schema switch), leaving the helper pointed at a closed instance. Because the failure mode is a quiet return on a data path rather than an error, an admin sees writes simply not happen.

title: DatabaseManager.createDatabaseBackup matches existing rows on columns[0] only, so backups collapse rows on composite keys
fix: Match on the table's real primary-key column set from the schema rather than assuming columns[0] is unique
tests: DatabaseManagerTest (startBackup_sqliteToSqlite_copiesData uses a single-column PK listed first, so it never exercises this)
observation: The backup writer decides insert-vs-update purely from the first column: `Object[] row = config.select(columns[0] + " = ?", new Object[]{objects[0]}, new int[]{dataTypes[0]}, new String[]{"*"});` and then updates with the same single-column predicate. For any table whose primary key is composite, or whose PK simply is not the first column in the column array, distinct source rows share a columns[0] value and each one updates the previously written row instead of inserting. The backup silently ends up with fewer rows than the source and with fields from the last-written row, i.e. corrupted backup data that only surfaces when someone restores from it.

title: AuditLogService and DatabaseFaultSink quote table identifiers with double quotes, which default-mode MySQL rejects
fix: Delegate identifier quoting to the backend dialect (backticks on MySQL) instead of hardcoding double quotes in the raw INSERT
tests: AuditLogServiceSqliteTest is SQLite-only; MysqlDialectTest is string-level and never touches these classes
observation: Both classes build their raw INSERT with `private static String quote(String identifier) { return '"' + identifier.replace("\"", "\"\"") + '"'; }` and the audit write is `"INSERT INTO " + quote(tableName) + " (timestamp, actor_uuid, action_type, payload) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)"`. MySQL only treats double-quoted text as an identifier under ANSI_QUOTES, which is not the default, so on a stock MySQL server every audit row and every persisted fault row fails with a syntax error caught by `catch (SQLException ex)` and reduced to a warn line. The class javadoc at line 150-153 openly concedes this ("if MySQL is run without ANSI_QUOTES, switch to backticks here"), so the audit trail and the fault sink are effectively dead on the default MySQL configuration while appearing configured. Same quote() duplicated at DatabaseFaultSink.java:114-116.

title: SQLite.switchSchema rebuilds the pool but never calls connect(), unlike MySQL.switchSchema
fix: Call connect() after replacing the HikariDataSource, matching MySQL.switchSchema
observation: SQLite.switchSchema ends with `disconnect(); this.dataSource = new HikariDataSource(config); return true;` — disconnect() nulls the `connection` field (line 135), and nothing re-establishes it. MySQL.switchSchema does the same swap but then calls `connect();` and repopulates tableNames (MySQL.java:105-106). After a SQLite schema switch the legacy Database is left with a live pool but a null connection, so the next schemaExists call throws "No connection established" and getConnection() returns null. This is in the @Deprecated(since=1.6.0) legacy stack scheduled for removal in 2.0.0, which is why it is tiered P2 rather than higher.

title: AbstractJdbcBackend.execute and query throw NullPointerException instead of SQLException when dataSource is null
fix: Null-check dataSource and throw SQLException("not connected") so the declared checked type is what callers actually get
observation: isConnected defends itself with `return dataSource != null && !dataSource.isClosed();` but the query methods do not: `try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection(); ...)` dereferences the field directly. Used before connect() or after a connect() that failed, these methods raise an unchecked NPE while declaring `throws SQLException`, so every caller that guards with `catch (SQLException)` — AuditLogService.write and DatabaseFaultSink among them — misses it and the NPE escapes to whatever scheduled task or command invoked it. The consequence is an unhandled stack trace on a path the code visibly intended to handle gracefully.

title: RepositoryRegistry.getTableName guesses a table name from the class name when reflection fails
fix: Report a fault and skip the repository instead of substituting a guessed table name
observation: When the no-arg instantiation of a Table class throws, the fallback is `return tableClass.getSimpleName().replace("Table", "").toLowerCase();` and the final fallback is the lowercased simple name. A Table whose real name does not match that derivation (a prefixed or pluralised table name, or a Table class needing constructor arguments) silently resolves to a name that exists in no schema, so the dependency decision above is made against a fabricated identifier. It is a latent trap today because the caller's own logic is already inverted (finding 1); fixing finding 1 without this one would make the guess load-bearing.

title: Legacy MySQL pools hardcode the removed com.mysql.jdbc.Driver class name
fix: Drop setDriverClassName and let DriverManager resolve, or use com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver
observation: Both the initial pool and switchSchema set `config.setDriverClassName("com.mysql.jdbc.Driver");` (lines 50 and 83). That class is deprecated in mysql-connector-j 8 and removed in 9, and HikariCP resolves the name eagerly via Class.forName, so on a server shipping a current connector the pool fails to initialise with a ClassNotFoundException at boot rather than falling back. Modern JDBC needs no explicit driver class at all. Legacy deprecated stack, hence P2.

title: Legacy SQLite and MySQL pools set minimumIdle(5), eagerly opening five native handles
fix: Set minimumIdle to a small value (or match maximumPoolSize semantics) so idle consumers do not hold five connections
observation: Both legacy pools configure `config.setMaximumPoolSize(10); config.setMinimumIdle(5);` in the initial pool and again in switchSchema. For SQLite this means five native file handles against the same .db file are opened at pool startup and held, which is what makes the database file undeletable on Windows after close — the consuming repo documents exactly this as a test-teardown hazard requiring CleanupMode.NEVER. For a plugin whose typical query load is bursty this is wasted handles rather than a correctness fault, so P2.

title: AbstractJdbcBackend.applySchema drops every live column the declared schema omits, destroying its data
fix: Never emit DROP COLUMN automatically; log the extra column and require an explicit opt-in or manual migration
tests: SchemaMigrationSqliteTest, SchemaConstraintsSqliteTest (cover ADD COLUMN, not the destructive DROP path)
observation: applySchema reconciles the live table against the declared schema and unconditionally destroys anything it does not recognise: `for (String drop : diff.toDrop()) { String dropSql = "ALTER TABLE " + quoteIdentifier(schema.tableName()) + " DROP COLUMN " + quoteIdentifier(drop); stmt.execute(dropSql); }`. SchemaDiff.diff builds toDrop as every live column name absent from the declared set (SchemaDiff.java:42-47), so a downgrade to an older plugin version whose schema lacks a newer column silently drops that column and all its rows' data on the next boot, as does any column an admin or a second plugin added to a shared table. There is no opt-out, no backup and no confirmation — the only trace is a `log.info("Schema migration: DROP COLUMN {}.{}", ...)` line after the data is already gone. Irreversible data loss on a routine version rollback is why this is the highest-tier finding in the system; also Oriel OR-DB-01, which observed it on MySQL.

title: AuditLogService and DatabaseFaultSink reduce a failed write to log.warn and never report it to Diagnostics
fix: Route the SQLException through Diagnostics/Fault so a failing audit or fault write appears in the diagnostics report
observation: The audit write ends `catch (SQLException ex) { log.warn("Failed to write audit row for {}/{}: {}", logName, actionType, ex.toString(), ex); }` and continues, with no Diagnostics.report call anywhere in the class; DatabaseFaultSink handles its own write failures the same way. An audit log exists precisely so that privileged actions are recoverable after the fact, so a silently dropped row is the one failure mode that must never be invisible — yet it never reaches the fault report an admin actually reads. This is the same swallow the repo's Result/Diagnostics rule forbids on a data path, and it compounds finding 4, which makes every one of these writes fail on a default MySQL server; also Oriel OR-DB-02.

title: DatabaseHandler.setType leaves type MYSQL with a null database when MySQL fails and SQLite fallback is disabled
fix: Fail fast when useSQLite declines to fall back — disable the plugin or throw rather than returning with a null database
observation: setType assigns `this.type = type;` up front, then runs `try { enforceType(MYSQL); } catch (RuntimeException exception) { useSQLite(getSchema()); }`. enforceType's MySQL branch nulls the field before rethrowing (`this.database = null; throw asPluginException(exception);`, and PluginException extends RuntimeException), and useSQLite opens with `if (!settings.isSqliteFailedMysql()) return;` — so an admin who deliberately disabled the fallback gets a silent early return leaving type == MYSQL and database == null. Boot then completes as if the database were configured and every later getDatabase() consumer dereferences null, so an ordinary MySQL outage turns into NullPointerExceptions on every persistence call instead of a clean startup failure. Filed P1 because the missing piece is a loud fail-fast rather than the crash itself; also Gangland CL-01, and still present at 1.9.1 despite the enforceType hardening.

title: AbstractRepository.saveAll snapshots the supplier's live collection on the caller's thread, so an async autosave copies a main-thread map
fix: Take the snapshot on the main thread before scheduling, or require the supplier to return an already-immutable copy
observation: saveAll copies with `List<T> snapshot = new ArrayList<>(collection);` before handing the snapshot to the async task, which is safe only when saveAll itself is called from the main thread. The autosave path does not guarantee that: RepositoryRegistry.saveAll walks its entries calling `repo.saveAllFromMemory(countDown)`, which resolves `saveAll(dataSupplier.get(), onComplete)` (AbstractRepository.java:149) — and a data supplier is conventionally a live view such as `() -> userMap.values()`. Driven from a consumer's asynchronous autosave timer, the ArrayList copy therefore iterates a map the main thread is still mutating, yielding a ConcurrentModificationException or a torn snapshot; the registry's `catch (Exception e) { log.error("Failed to save data for repository: {}", ...) }` swallows it into one line and that repository's data is simply never written. Nothing in the API documents a main-thread requirement; also Gangland CL-02.

title: AbstractJdbcBackend.applySchema adds NOT NULL columns without a DEFAULT, so SQLite rejects every ADD on a populated table
fix: When a diff-added column is NOT NULL with no default, emit a type-appropriate DEFAULT (legacy Table.inferDefault parity) or add it nullable
tests: TableSchemaAdapterSqliteTest (sidesteps it: the added column is setCanBeNull(true) with the comment "SQLite rejects ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL without a default on a non-empty table")
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] The ADD path emits `" ADD COLUMN " + renderColumn(add)`, and renderColumn appends `" NOT NULL"` for any non-nullable column but a DEFAULT only `if (column.defaultValue() != null)` (lines 297-301). TableSchemas.fromAttribute maps nullability from Attribute.isCanBeNull(), whose field defaults to false (Attribute.java:23), so every ORM attribute a consumer adds without explicitly calling setCanBeNull(true) or setDefaultValue arrives as NOT NULL with no default. Verified against sqlite-jdbc 3.49: `ALTER TABLE "t" ADD COLUMN "level" INTEGER NOT NULL` on a one-row table fails with "Cannot add a NOT NULL column with default value NULL", so applySchema throws and RepositoryRegistry.createTables rethrows it (lines 286-288) on the first release that adds a column, which is the case the diff engine exists for. The legacy Table.buildColumnDefinition covers this with `def.append(" DEFAULT ").append(inferDefault(attribute.getType()))` (Table.java:446-449), so moving a repository onto the backend SPI regresses it; MySQL is hit too for TIMESTAMP NOT NULL columns under the default NO_ZERO_DATE strict mode.

title: DatabaseManager backup copies rows positionally between two independently ordered column lists
fix: Read the source with the target's column list (or map values by column name) instead of pairing source-physical values with target-physical columns, and catch RuntimeException per row
tests: DatabaseManagerTest (source and target are built from the same TestTable, so their column orders always match)
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] databaseInformation reads each source table with `String[] columns = config.getColumns()...` then `info.addAll(config.selectAll(columns));` (lines 91-95), i.e. in the source's physical column order, while backupAllDatabases re-derives `String[] columns = config.getColumns()` from the target (line 145) and writes `config.insert(columns, objects, dataTypes)` positionally. Legacy validateSchema appends new columns at the physical end with ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN, whereas a backup target created fresh by handler.initialize() uses attribute order, so any table that gained a non-trailing attribute in an upgrade has two different orders and values land in the wrong columns; same-typed columns (two INTEGER counters) swap silently. When the counts differ Database.insert throws IllegalArgumentException (Database.java:258-259), and a type mismatch throws ClassCastException at `(LocalDateTime) value` (Database.java:740); neither is caught by the per-row `catch (SQLException exception)` (line 172), so runQueries' Throwable catch abandons every remaining table while startBackup still logs "Backup done". Distinct from row 3 (columns[0] matching).

title: MysqlBackend hardcodes com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver, which Spigot 1.16.5 and 1.17.x do not bundle
fix: Return null from driverClassName() so Hikari resolves the server-bundled driver from the jdbc:mysql URL through DriverManager
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] `protected String driverClassName() { ... return "com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver"; }` is passed to `config.setDriverClassName(driverClass)` in AbstractJdbcBackend.connect (lines 52-53), and HikariConfig.setDriverClassName throws a RuntimeException ("Failed to load driver class ...") when the class is absent. Keystone's API floor is Spigot 1.16.5, and the local spigot-1.16.5 and spigot-1.17.1 server jars contain com/mysql/jdbc/Driver.class (Connector/J 5.1) but no com/mysql/cj/jdbc/Driver.class; Connector/J 8 is only bundled from 1.18. So on the floor versions the new MysqlBackend can never connect, and every MySQL consumer migrated to the backend SPI fails at connect, while the class javadoc says it "Uses the server-bundled" cj driver. AbstractJdbcBackend already guards `if (driverClass != null)`, so no class name is needed; this is the mirror image of row 8 (legacy MySQL pinned to the old name, which newer servers drop).

title: AbstractJdbcBackend.connect lets HikariCP's unchecked pool-init failure escape its throws SQLException contract
fix: Wrap setDriverClassName and new HikariDataSource(config) and rethrow a RuntimeException as SQLException, as DatabaseHandler.enforceType does for the legacy stack
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] connect ends with `this.dataSource = new HikariDataSource(config);`, and with Hikari's default initializationFailTimeout an unreachable MySQL makes that constructor throw HikariPool.PoolInitializationException, a RuntimeException; a missing driver class likewise throws RuntimeException from setDriverClassName (line 53). DatabaseBackend.connect documents only `throws SQLException`, so a consumer that follows the contract with `catch (SQLException)` to fall back to SQLite or disable persistence never sees the failure: it escapes into bean creation and an ordinary database outage takes the whole boot down. The legacy DatabaseHandler.enforceType catches `SQLException | RuntimeException` for exactly this reason (its javadoc: driver-level problems "surface as unchecked HikariCP exceptions"), so the backend SPI regressed it. Sibling of row 6 (NPE instead of SQLException in execute/query).

title: DatabaseFaultSink.accept runs a blocking JDBC insert on whatever thread reported the fault
fix: Hand the insert to a bounded async queue or executor (drop on full) instead of calling backend.execute inline from accept
tests: DatabaseFaultSinkSqliteTest (in-memory SQLite only, never an unreachable pool)
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] Diagnostics.deliver calls `sink.accept(fault)` synchronously on the reporting thread (Diagnostics.java:89-92), and accept does `backend.execute(sql, ...)` inline, which borrows a pooled connection with a 30 s connectionTimeout (AbstractJdbcBackend.java:64). SQLException is classified DEPENDENCY (DefaultClassifiers.java:49-51), exactly the kind this sink persists, so during a MySQL outage every reported database fault triggers another blocking connection attempt: a main-thread caller such as JdbcQueryBuilder.list (which reports "backend.query" before rethrowing) waits up to 30 s for its own query and then up to another 30 s inside the sink. In normal operation it still adds a synchronous database round trip to the reporting thread for every INTERNAL_BUG/DEPENDENCY fault. The outage is the moment faults are frequent, so a database blip becomes watchdog-length tick stalls.

title: AbstractRepository.runBackendAsync skips onComplete when the work throws anything but SQLException
fix: Catch RuntimeException too (report it) and run onComplete in a finally block, matching DatabaseHelper.runQueries' Throwable catch
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] The backend branch runs `try { work.run(); } catch (SQLException exception) { reportBackendFailure("repository.save", exception); } if (onComplete != null) onComplete.run();`, so any unchecked exception, such as an NPE from a consumer's getData/processSave on one bad entity or the UnsupportedOperationException DatabaseBackend.upsert's default throws for a custom backend, bypasses both the Diagnostics report and onComplete. RepositoryRegistry.saveAll(onComplete) counts repositories down through exactly this callback (`repo.saveAllFromMemory(countDown)`, RepositoryRegistry.java:251-252), so one such failure in an async autosave means the registry-level completion never fires and whatever the consumer chained on it (a shutdown or kick sequence, a "save finished" notice) waits forever, with the exception visible only as a scheduler stack trace. The legacy branch has no such gap because DatabaseHelper.runQueries catches Throwable before runQueriesOnComplete runs onComplete.

title: RepositoryRegistry.invokeCondition resolves condition classes with Class.forName, ignoring the scan ClassLoader
fix: Pass the scan classLoader into invokeCondition and use Class.forName(className, true, classLoader)
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] scanAndRegisterRepositories(basePackage, classLoader) exists (since 1.8.0) so a module jar's repositories are discovered through its own loader, but the condition check it runs, `boolean invoke = invokeCondition(condition);` (line 97), does `Class<?> clazz = Class.forName(className);`, which resolves against RepositoryRegistry's own defining loader (Keystone's plugin loader). A ModuleClassLoader is not a plugin loader, so a module repository declaring `@Repository(condition = "<module class>.enabled()")` hits ClassNotFoundException, invokeCondition logs "Failed to invoke condition" and returns false, and the repository is skipped on every boot even when its condition holds. Unconditional module repositories are unaffected, which is why only the conditional ones silently go missing.

title: RepositoryRegistry iterates a ConcurrentHashMap for saveAll and migrateSchema, discarding the dependency order it records
fix: Keep repositories in insertion order (LinkedHashMap, or iterate by registrationOrder) so saveAll, the migrate pass and getAllRepositories run parent-before-child
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] repositories is `new ConcurrentHashMap<>()` keyed by entity Class (line 51), and saveAll, the migrateSchema loop (line 293) and getAllRepositories, whose javadoc says "Get all registered repositories in registration order", all iterate `repositories.values()` in hash order; `registrationOrder` is written at lines 132 and 497 and never read. Tables declare FOREIGN KEYs (TableSchemas.fromTable and legacy createTableQuery), which InnoDB enforces. On shutdown the saves run inline in that arbitrary order, so if a child repository flushes first, a child row whose parent was created since the last autosave violates the FK and, because the batch upsert is one transaction, the whole child batch rolls back and is lost at stop; during play the async saves race the same way and only self-heal on a later cycle. SQLite does not enforce FKs, so this surfaces on MySQL only. Separate from row 1, which breaks the sort whose order this map then discards.

title: SchemaMigrations.rebuildSqliteTable copies with INSERT OR IGNORE, silently dropping rows that violate the new DDL
fix: Use a plain INSERT so a constraint violation rolls the rebuild back, or compare copied and source row counts and fail on a shortfall
tests: SchemaMigrationsTest (both fixture rows satisfy the new constraints; no violating-row case)
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] The rebuild runs `stmt.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO " + tempName + " (" + columns + ") " + "SELECT " + columns + " FROM " + tableName);` and then unconditionally `stmt.execute("DROP TABLE " + tableName);` and commits. SQLite's OR IGNORE resolution skips any row that violates a UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL or CHECK constraint of the replacement table, so a legacy row with a NULL in a column the new DDL makes NOT NULL, or two rows colliding on the new key, are discarded with no error, count or log line, and the original table holding them is dropped in the same transaction. The javadoc promises the method "copies the specified columns over" and that a mid-flight failure "rolls back cleanly", but constraint violations are turned from failures into silent, irreversible row loss.

title: TableBackend.insert/update/delete/selectAll emit bare identifiers while applySchema and upsert quote them
fix: Quote table and column names through the backend dialect (expose quoteIdentifier or route reads through BackendQueryBuilder) in every TableBackend statement
tests: TableBackendSqliteTest (fixture column names are not keywords)
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] applySchema, upsert/upsertAll and where() all go through the dialect's quoteIdentifier, so a table with a column named after an SQL keyword (`rank`, reserved in MySQL 8, or `order`/`key`/`group` on either dialect) is created and upserted successfully. The remaining statements concatenate raw names: `"INSERT INTO " + table.getName() + " (" + String.join(", ", cols) + ")..."`, `sql.append(setCols.get(i)).append(" = ?")` and `"SELECT " + String.join(", ", cols) + " FROM " + table.getName()`. On such a table selectAll, the call the class javadoc and AbstractRepository.tableBackend() point doLoadAll at, fails with a syntax error; AbstractRepository.loadAll reports it and returns an empty collection, so the plugin boots as if the table were empty while the upsert path keeps writing to it.

title: MysqlBackend never enables rewriteBatchedStatements, so upsertAll still costs one round trip per row
fix: Add config.addDataSourceProperty("rewriteBatchedStatements", "true") in MysqlBackend.applyExtraConfig
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] DatabaseBackend.upsertAll's javadoc states "flushing hundreds of dirty entities must not pay one round trip per row", and AbstractJdbcBackend implements it as a JDBC batch (`stmt.addBatch()` then `stmt.executeBatch()`, lines 169-176). MySQL Connector/J only collapses a batch into multi-row statements when rewriteBatchedStatements=true; without it executeBatch sends each INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE separately.
