MysqlBackend.applyExtraConfig sets only `useSSL`, so on MySQL an autosave of N rows is still N network round trips (inside one transaction), the cost the SPI method was added to remove; SQLite is unaffected. Performance only, hence P3.

title: Legacy Table.recreateTableSQLite copies only declared attributes, dropping kept undeclared columns and their data
fix: Carry every live column not in the declaration into the rebuilt table (definition from PRAGMA table_info) or refuse the rebuild and report a fault
observation: [found 2026-09-24 by the review follow-up fixer, verified by the orchestrator] validateSchema calls recreateTableSQLite(database) on a nullability mismatch; it builds the new table from `createTableQuery(database)` and copies `String cols = String.join(", ", attributes.keySet());` then `DROP TABLE tmpName`. Since KS-DB-10 (1.11.2) validateSchema deliberately keeps undeclared live columns, but this rebuild path still discards them: any consumer on the legacy stack that changes one attribute's nullability loses every kept column's data on the next boot, contradicting the keep-by-default contract.

title: ModuleLoader.purgeStale lets one undeletable stale jar abort discovery of every module in the folder
fix: Wrap the marker loop's deleteIfExists calls in a per-file try/catch that logs, mirroring the stale-directory loop above it
observation: The first loop deletes each file in `.stale/` defensively, catching IOException per file and only warning. The second loop does not: `if (Files.deleteIfExists(jar)) { log.info(...); } Files.deleteIfExists(marker);` runs bare, and discover() wraps the whole purgeStale() call in a single try/catch that reports FAULT_FOLDER "Modules folder is not usable" and returns. On Windows a stale jar still held open by a previous run (the classloader handle problem this project already documents) throws IOException here, so one leftover file makes the host plugin load zero modules instead of skipping that one file. The asymmetry with the loop three lines above shows the per-file tolerance was the intent.

title: ArtifactCoordinate.jarFileName builds a filename from unsanitized Maven coordinates, letting a repository escape the modules folder
fix: Reject coordinates containing path separators or "..", and verify the resolved target stays inside targetDirectory
observation: jarFileName() is `requireVersion(); return artifactId + "-" + version + ".jar";` with no character validation, and ArtifactResolver.download() feeds it straight to the filesystem: `Path target = targetDirectory.resolve(coordinate.jarFileName());` (ArtifactResolver.java:100). For an update download the version half comes from the remote maven-metadata.xml via MavenMetadata, so the value is controlled by whatever repository the admin configured — a compromised or hostile mirror can return a version containing `../` (or an absolute path, which resolve() honours outright) and place the downloaded jar anywhere the server process can write. Filed P1 rather than P0 because it requires a hostile repository rather than firing on a normal update.

title: ModuleUpdateService.downloadNow retires the working jar before confirming the download is a usable module
fix: Validate the downloaded jar's module.yml and Id before calling retire() on the installed jar
observation: The only gate before replacement is `if (downloaded.isFailure()) return downloaded;` followed immediately by `retire(update.installedJar());`, which moves the currently-working jar into `.stale/`. isFailure covers I/O errors and a SHA-256 mismatch against the repository's own checksum, so it proves the bytes match what the repository published — not that they are a valid module with the right module.yml, matching Id and a KeystoneModule main class. A repository publishing a bad-but-correctly-checksummed jar therefore costs the admin the working module, and the failure only becomes visible on the next restart.

title: ModuleUpdateService.pending is updated by an unsynchronized read-modify-write across async download tasks
fix: Guard the pending mutation with a lock, or use an AtomicReference update loop
observation: The update is a three-step read-modify-write on a plain volatile field: `List<ModuleUpdate> remaining = new ArrayList<>(pending); remaining.removeIf(candidate -> candidate.moduleId().equals(update.moduleId())); pending = List.copyOf(remaining);`. Downloads normally run on their own async task, so two overlapping downloads (an admin retrying a slow one, or two modules updating together) can both read the same snapshot and the second write loses the first's removal. The consequence is a stale entry left in the pending list, so an already-downloaded update is offered again; volatile makes the field visible but does nothing for the compound update.

title: ModuleLoader.instantiate reports a module's failing static initializer as "Main missing"
fix: Separate the LinkageError case from ClassNotFoundException and report the initializer failure with its own message
observation: Class loading uses `Class.forName(descriptor.mainClass(), true, classLoader)` with initialize=true, and the handler is `catch (ClassNotFoundException | LinkageError exception)` reporting FAULT_MAIN_MISSING with the text "names Main X, which is not in its jar". A main class whose static initializer throws raises ExceptionInInitializerError, a LinkageError, so an admin whose module has a perfectly present Main class but a broken static block is told the class is absent. The underlying cause is attached via .cause(exception), but the headline message sends the admin looking for a packaging problem that does not exist.

title: ModuleResolution reports only the first missing Plugins entry per module
fix: Collect every unsatisfied plugin for the module before breaking, or drop the break and deduplicate the removal
observation: The plugins check is `if (pluginEnabled.test(plugin)) continue; accepted.remove(descriptor.id()); faults.add(...); break;` — the break ends the scan at the first unsatisfied entry. A module declaring `Plugins: [Bartizan, Vault]` with both absent surfaces only "needs plugin Bartizan", so an admin installs Bartizan, restarts, and is then told about Vault. Correct module gating either way; this costs an extra restart cycle per additional missing plugin.

title: A module bean body that hits a deleted host member crashes the whole host bootstrap instead of skipping that module
fix: Give the host a per-module guard once beans start: catch LinkageError (NoSuchMethodError/NoSuchFieldError/NoClassDefFoundError) thrown from a module @Bean body or module listener/command construction, report it as a module fault (e.g. module.bean.failed with the module id and jar) and drop that module and its dependants, instead of letting IllegalStateException escape BeanFactory.instantiate(); needs rollback-capable registration in keystone-bean, so it is a Keystone phase of its own. Until then the gangland-api contract + minor-compatible Host_Api are the prevention.
location: keystone-bean/src/main/java/org/luckyraven/keystone/bean/BeanFactory.java:488-492 (invokeBean rethrows InvocationTargetException as IllegalStateException) + keystone-module/src/main/java/org/luckyraven/keystone/module/ModuleLoader.java:176-187 (the last per-module catch)
observation: ModuleLoader isolates instantiate/configure/onEnabled per module (catch Throwable at ModuleLoader.java:176-187, :204-210) and ReflectionGuard (1.9.1) skips a scanned class whose SIGNATURE names an absent type, but nothing guards a module bean BODY: a module compiled against a newer host that calls a method the running host lacks throws NoSuchMethodError inside method.invoke, BeanFactory.invokeBean wraps it as IllegalStateException, and the host plugin (Gangland.onEnable at Gangland.java:91-96 has no try/catch around context.bootstrap()) is disabled by Bukkit - every module and the core go down for one stale module jar. Found 2026-09-10 by the module-API wave research (agent A section 2.2); not reproduced on a server.

title: Unquoted Host_Api: 1.10 parses as YAML float 1.1, collapsing the Host_Api minor floor
fix: Reject a non-String Host_Api scalar with a descriptor fault telling the author to quote it (or read the raw node), and validate Host_Api against \d+(\.\d+)? so garbage no longer parses as 0.0
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] parse reads `String hostApi = yaml.getString("Host_Api");`, and Bukkit's YamlConfiguration returns the SnakeYAML-typed scalar stringified, so the documented unquoted form (`Host_Api: 0.8` in docs/keystone-module.md and every test) is a Double. Verified against spigot-api 1.16.5: `Host_Api: 1.10` reads back as "1.1" and `1.20` as "1.2". ModuleDescriptor.isCompatibleWith (ModuleDescriptor.java:73-75, `required.minor() <= host.minor()`) then sees minor 1, so a module built for host 0.10 is accepted on any 0.1-0.9 host instead of refused (Gangland's host line is 0.9 today, so its next minor is exactly this case), and the module then fails at runtime with NoSuchMethodError (see row 7). The same coercion truncates a two-part `Version: 0.10` (line 76) to 0.1, breaking duplicate resolution and update comparisons, and a non-numeric Host_Api such as `latest` parses as 0.0 and passes the floor on every 0.x host because nothing validates the format.

title: downloadNow retires the working jar for an update whose Host_Api the host cannot load
fix: Before retire(), refuse with module.update.invalid when the downloaded descriptor fails isCompatibleWith(hostApi) (pass the host api into ModuleUpdateService), and skip such releases in checkNow
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] The KS-MO-03 gate checks only `descriptor == null || !descriptor.id().equals(update.moduleId())` and then runs `retire(update.installedJar());`. checkNow chose the release purely by `PluginVersion.parse(newest.get()).compareTo(descriptor.parsedVersion()) > 0` (line 98), so the newest release is offered even when it was built for a newer host minor. Downloading it moves the working jar into .stale/ (deleted by the next discover), and on restart ModuleResolution drops the new jar with module.host.incompatible, leaving the admin with no module at all until the host is upgraded. The downloaded descriptor is already parsed at line 127, so the Host_Api (and Plugins) check is one condition. This is not a re-file of row 3 (KS-MO-03): that fix covers a wrong Id, not an incompatible jar with the right Id.

title: downloadNow deletes the module when the download target equals the installed jar path
fix: Skip retire() (and the wrong-Id deleteQuietly) when the downloaded path is the installed jar (normalized equals or Files.isSameFile), and refuse a download whose descriptor Version is not newer than the installed one
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] The resolver names the download `artifactId + "-" + version + ".jar"` and moves it over any existing file (ArtifactResolver.java:100 `Path target = targetDirectory.resolve(coordinate.jarFileName());`, :152 `move(part, target)` with REPLACE_EXISTING), then downloadNow unconditionally calls `retire(update.installedJar())`. When the hand-written module.yml Version lags the Maven version, the jar the service installed last time is named e.g. foo-1.2.0.jar while its descriptor says 1.1.0, so every check re-offers 1.2.0 and the next download targets that same path. On Linux the move replaces the open jar, the identity check passes, and retire() moves the fresh download into .stale/, which the next discover() deletes, so the module disappears. The wrong-Id branch has the same hole: `deleteQuietly(jar)` deletes the path that was the installed jar. On Windows the replace fails on the locked jar and surfaces as module.artifact.io instead.

title: checkNow re-lists an already-downloaded update as pending until the restart
fix: Remember the module ids downloaded this session and exclude them from checkNow's result while restartRequired is true
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] checkNow rebuilds pending wholesale from the LoadedModule descriptors (`pending = List.copyOf(updates);`), which keep the pre-download Version until the restart. After downloadNow removed the entry, any later check (a periodic check task or an admin re-running the check command) puts it back, so pending(), documented as "Updates found by the last check that have not been downloaded yet", offers the same download again, and a host that auto-applies pending re-downloads it on every cycle. The damage is bounded because the second download overwrites the same file, but it is operator-visible noise and wasted bandwidth.

title: NpcCombatDelegate.attackEntity never consults the targetFilter SPI that attack(Player) enforces
fix: Add the same owner.targetFilter().isAttackable(target) guard to attackEntity that attack(Player) already applies
observation: attack(Player) opens with `if (player.isDead() || !owner.targetFilter().isAttackable(player)) return;` but the entity-typed sibling opens with only `if (target.isDead()) return;` and never calls owner.targetFilter() anywhere in its body. NpcTargetFilter is the SPI through which a consumer expresses what its NPC may not hit — allied gang members, civilians, protected mobs — so any consumer path that routes through attackEntity rather than attack(Player) has its protection silently skipped. The NPC then damages entities the consumer explicitly marked unattackable, which is exactly the product decision the layering rules push out to the SPI.

title: AbstractNpc.destroy skips despawn and the onDespawn callback when rangedAttack.onDestroy throws
fix: Wrap rangedAttack.onDestroy() in its own try/catch so a failing SPI cannot skip the despawn callback
observation: destroy() runs `rangedAttack.onDestroy();` as the first statement inside the try, before the `if (npc.isSpawned())` block that fires the onDespawn consumer callback and `npc.despawn()`. A consumer's ranged-attack SPI implementation that throws there skips both, and the finally block only covers cleanupTransientState() and npc.destroy(). The onDespawn callback is documented one line above as the caller's chance to "release entity-keyed state (marks, registries, ...)", so a throwing SPI permanently leaks that consumer state while the NPC itself is still destroyed — an inconsistent half-teardown rather than a clean failure.

title: NpcNavigationDelegate leaves ladderClimbActive set when the entity is transiently null, stalling navigation permanently
fix: Check and clear ladderClimbActive before the entity==null early return in updateNavigationProgress
observation: updateNavigationProgress reads `LivingEntity entity = owner.getEntity(); if (entity == null) { return; }` and only afterwards tests `if (ladderClimbActive) { tickLadderClimb(); return; }`, so a null entity during a climb skips the tick that would normally end it and the flag stays true. That flag then disables all recovery: stopNavigation is `if (ladderClimbActive) return; owner.npc.getNavigator().cancelNavigation(); resetNavigationTracking();` (line 216-219), so it returns without cancelling anything. Citizens reporting a momentarily null entity — a chunk unload or a despawn/respawn cycle — therefore leaves that NPC unable to navigate for the rest of its life, and its gravity restoration in resetNavigationTracking never runs either.

title: EntitySpawner.findSpawnLocation loops forever on the main thread when getSpawnRadiusShrinkStep returns zero or negative
fix: Validate the shrink step is greater than zero before the loop and fall back to a sane default
observation: The phase-2 search is `for (double max = maxDist; max >= minDist; max -= shrinkStep)` where `double shrinkStep = config.getSpawnRadiusShrinkStep();` comes straight from the consumer's SpawnConfigProvider with no bounds check. A value of 0 never decrements max, and a negative value increases it, so the loop never terminates while running on the main server thread — the whole server hangs and the watchdog eventually kills it. The trigger is a single mistyped spawn-radius value in a consumer's NPC YAML, and nothing between the config read and the loop rejects it.

title: NpcCombatDelegate.faceTarget normalizes a possibly zero-length vector, producing a NaN facing direction
fix: Guard with lengthSquared() == 0 (or use Vector#isZero) before normalize and skip the facing update
observation: faceTarget computes `Vector direction = player.getEyeLocation().toVector().subtract(shooterEye.toVector()).normalize();` with no length check, then feeds it to `entity.getLocation().setDirection(direction)` and teleports the NPC there. Bukkit's normalize divides by the vector length, so coincident eye positions — an NPC and target teleported onto the same spot, or both pathed into one block — yield NaN components and a teleport to a non-finite location, which Bukkit rejects with IllegalArgumentException. faceTarget runs unconditionally at the top of every attack, and faceTargetEntity plus the melee knockback calculation repeat the same unguarded normalize.

title: resetNavigationTracking's ladderClimbActive branch is unreachable from its only caller
fix: Restore gravity where the climb actually ends, or drop the unreachable branch once finding 3 is fixed
observation: resetNavigationTracking contains `if (ladderClimbActive) { LivingEntity entity = owner.getEntity(); if (entity != null) { entity.setGravity(true); } }`, but its caller stopNavigation returns early precisely when that flag is set, so the branch cannot run from that path. The gravity restoration it performs is therefore not reachable where it was intended to matter, which is the same root confusion as finding 3 — the flag guards both the cleanup and the caller that would perform it. Cosmetically dead today; it should be resolved together with finding 3 rather than deleted blindly.

title: EntitySpawner behind/visibility checks treat Bukkit yaw as a math angle, off by 90 degrees
fix: Compare against the Minecraft facing angle (Math.toRadians(yaw) + PI/2, or a dot product with Location#getDirection()) in both isSpawnBehindPlayer and isVisibleToOtherPlayers
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] isSpawnBehindPlayer does `double playerYaw = Math.toRadians(playerLoc.getYaw());` and `double toSpawnAngle = Math.atan2(spawnLoc.getZ() - playerLoc.getZ(), spawnLoc.getX() - playerLoc.getX());` and treats angleDiff > PI/2 as behind. atan2(dz, dx) is measured from +X, but Bukkit yaw 0 faces +Z (direction (-sin yaw, cos yaw)), so the reference is off by exactly 90 degrees: for a player facing south the "behind" half-plane is the -X half, and half of that is in front of the player. isVisibleToOtherPlayers (lines 119-123) has the identical error, so a location straight ahead of another player is 90 degrees off its 60-degree cone and reported unseen. In normal play, phase-1 spawns land in the player's field of view and despawns happen in plain sight of bystanders. NpcNavigationDelegate.navigateTo (line 207) and findForwardWanderDestination (lines 375-376) already use the correct `-sin`/`cos` convention, which confirms the intent.

title: isNavigationHopeless is always false after the first navigateTo; navPlan never empties
fix: Test plan exhaustion (navPlanStep >= navPlan.size()) instead of navPlan.isEmpty(), and clear navPlan in resetNavigationTracking and on exhaustion
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] isNavigationHopeless opens with `if (!navPlan.isEmpty()) return false;`. navPlan changes only through `navPlan.clear();` followed by `navPlan.addAll(buildNavPlan(destination));` on replan (lines 117-121), and buildNavPlan always appends at least the final NONE step (line 1094). Plan exhaustion only nulls navPlanTarget, and resetNavigationTracking never touches navPlan. After the first navigateTo the list is therefore permanently non-empty, and the method always returns false whatever consecutiveStuckChecks says. Gangland's PursuingBehavior (`if (cop.isNavigationHopeless()) { cop.transitionTo(CopState.RETURNING); ...`) and the civilian combat/flee behaviours rely on it, so an NPC chasing an unreachable target never gives up and stays stuck, and the hopeless fallback those consumers gate on it never runs.

title: scaleCooldown's 5-tick floor equals the melee base, so HARD and DEADLY never speed melee
fix: Put the floor below the base (e.g. Math.max(scaled, 1) or a separate minimum constant), or raise the melee base so the multiplier has room
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] `int scaled = (int) Math.round(baseCooldown * owner.difficulty.getFireRateMultiplier()); return Math.max(scaled, 5);` is called with base 5 from both melee paths (`owner.attackCooldown = scaleCooldown(5);` at lines 190 and 209). HARD (0.85 -> 4) and DEADLY (0.7 -> 4) both clamp back to 5, the same as NORMAL, so the fireRateMultiplier that NpcDifficulty's javadoc says multiplies "the melee perform-* paths" can only slow melee (EASY) and never speeds it up. Only the vanilla-ranged base of 15 actually varies across the faster tiers.

title: NpcMarkManager caches marks by entity UUID with no eviction for dead or unloaded entities
fix: Drop the cache (a PDC read is cheap), or evict on death/removal, e.g. key a WeakHashMap by Entity
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] setMark does `entityMarks.put(entity.getUniqueId(), mark);` and getMark caches every persisted mark it reads (`entityMarks.put(entity.getUniqueId(), markStr);`), but the only removals are removeMark and onClear/clearCache on reload. An entity that is marked and then killed, removed by the server or unloaded with its chunk keeps its entry until the next reload. A server that marks every spawned cop or civilian therefore grows the HashMap for its whole uptime. Keystone offers no eviction hook, and AbstractNpc.destroy's onDespawn callback only covers entities torn down through that path. Each entry is small, but the map is unbounded.

title: NpcNavigationConfig.getMinRepathAfterLossTicks is required of consumers but never read
fix: Wire it into the path-loss re-path throttle it documents, or deprecate it
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] The interface requires `int getMinRepathAfterLossTicks();`, documented as the minimum AI ticks before "a path-loss recovery re-path is allowed", but no class in keystone-npc calls it: AbstractNpc reads getAiTickRate and NpcNavigationDelegate's constructor reads the other knobs. Gangland still parses `Min_Repath_After_Loss_Ticks` from settings.yml (Settings.java:606) and forwards it through GanglandCopSettings, so admins tune a key that has no effect.

title: EconomyHandler.setAmount discards both Vault EconomyResponses, creating or destroying money when either leg fails
fix: Check transactionSuccess() on the withdraw before depositing, and abort (or compensate) when either response fails
tests: EconomyHandlerTest (userMode_setAmountWithdrawsEverythingThenDepositsTheNewBalance pins the call order without asserting response handling)
observation: setAmount implements "set the balance" as a withdraw-everything-then-deposit-the-new-value pair and throws away both return values: `vaultEconomy.withdrawPlayer(offlinePlayer, vaultEconomy.getBalance(offlinePlayer)); vaultEconomy.depositPlayer(offlinePlayer, this.amount.doubleValue());`. Vault reports failure through the returned EconomyResponse rather than by throwing, so when the backing economy plugin refuses the withdraw — a frozen or bank-backed account, a plugin-side limit, a race with another transaction — the deposit still runs and the player keeps their old balance plus the new amount, creating money out of nothing. The mirror case destroys it: a successful withdraw followed by a rejected deposit leaves the account at zero. The pair is also non-atomic, so a server crash or exception between the two calls loses the whole balance, and every consumer that sets a balance through this class inherits the fault.

title: EconomyHandler.depositAmount accepts a negative delta, bypassing withdrawAmount's insufficient-funds guard
fix: Reject negative deltas in depositAmount (throw EconomyException) so every debit routes through withdrawAmount's balance check
observation: depositAmount is simply `setAmount(getAmount().add(Currency.of(delta)));` with no sign validation, while the sibling withdrawAmount explicitly guards with `if (normalised.compareTo(current) > 0) throw new EconomyException("Amount exceeding balance");`. Currency.of only rescales the value (`return raw.setScale(SCALE, ROUNDING_MODE);`) and never rejects a negative, so a mis-signed refund or penalty delta debits the account through the path that has no balance check and can drive the computed balance below zero. setAmount then withdraws everything and calls depositPlayer with a negative amount, which most Vault economies reject outright, leaving the player at zero with their original balance gone. Filed P1 rather than P0 because it takes a caller passing a negative delta, but the consequence is real money loss.

title: EconomyHandler gates on vaultEconomy != null but never on vaultEconomy.isEnabled()
fix: Check isEnabled() alongside the null check, matching VaultEconomyProvider.isAvailable()
observation: getAmount() and setAmount() both gate purely on `useUserInfo() && vaultEconomy != null`, treating a non-null reference as a working economy. VaultEconomyProvider.isAvailable() treats isEnabled() as the real availability signal for the very same Economy type (VaultEconomyProvider.java:39-41), so the two classes disagree about what "the economy is usable" means. If the economy plugin behind Vault is present but disabled, balance reads return whatever the disabled provider yields and writes go into a provider that is not accepting them, with no error surfaced to the caller.

title: VaultEconomyProvider, VaultGroupProvider and VaultPermissionProvider do not fail closed on a throwing Vault backend
fix: Wrap the Vault calls in try/catch that reports through Diagnostics and returns the fail-closed value, as VaultOfflinePermissionService already does
observation: withdraw and deposit call `economy.withdrawPlayer(...)` / `economy.depositPlayer(...)` with no guard, and VaultGroupProvider.inGroup/primaryGroup plus VaultPermissionProvider.add/remove do the same. The one class in this package that does defend itself is VaultOfflinePermissionService, which wraps its lookups in try/catch and reports through Diagnostics — so the fail-closed pattern is established house style and these four are the gap. A third-party permission or economy plugin throwing from its Vault implementation therefore propagates out of Keystone into whatever consumer call site was running, instead of degrading to a denied permission or a reported fault.

title: EconomyHandler.vaultEconomy is a non-volatile static read and written without synchronization
fix: Mark the field volatile so a runtime setVaultEconomy is visible to other threads
tests: EconomyHandlerTest (saveStatic/restoreStatic treat it as a server-global fact but do not exercise cross-thread visibility)
observation: `private static Economy vaultEconomy;` carries Lombok-generated static accessors and is read on every getAmount()/setAmount() while being settable at any time via setVaultEconomy(...). The static itself is legitimate under the shared-classloader rule — the server's Vault economy is a server-global fact, the explicitly permitted case — so the only defect is the missing volatile, which leaves a late or re-registered economy potentially invisible to a thread that already cached the field. Economy calls are expected on the main thread, so this is a memory-model tidiness issue rather than an observed fault.

title: EconomyHandler.withdrawAmount accepts a negative delta and credits the account
fix: Reject normalised.signum() < 0 in withdrawAmount (and in depositAmount per #2) with EconomyException
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] withdrawAmount only checks `if (normalised.compareTo(current) > 0) throw new EconomyException("Amount exceeding balance");`, which a negative delta always passes, then runs `setAmount(current.subtract(normalised))`, so withdrawing -100 adds 100. This is the mirror of #2 (a negative deposit), and #2's fix direction only touches depositAmount. A concrete trigger exists today: Gangland's GangWithdrawCommand parses `Currency.parse(args[2])` from the player's command, checks only `gang.getEconomy().getAmount().compareTo(argAmount) < 0` (false for a negative amount), then calls `gang.getEconomy().withdrawAmount(argAmount)`, so `/gang withdraw -1000` inflates the gang vault. Keystone's balance guard is the only sign check on this path.

title: Currency.parse accepts huge exponents, so one command argument can freeze the server
fix: Reject exponent notation (or bound precision()/scale() before setScale) and return a USER_ERROR instead of computing the value
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] parse does `new BigDecimal(cleaned).setScale(SCALE, ROUNDING_MODE)` on raw player input. BigDecimal accepts `1e20000000`, and setScale(2) then materialises a 66-million-bit unscaled integer: measured at about 6 s of CPU for 1e20000000 and 0.8 s for 1e5000000, with cost rising faster than linearly, so a larger exponent reaches the 60 s Spigot watchdog. A negative exponent such as `1e-999999999` instead throws `ArithmeticException: BigInteger would overflow supported range`, an unchecked exception that callers catching only NumberFormatException do not handle. Gangland passes command arguments straight in (`BigDecimal argAmount = Currency.parse(args[2]);` in GangWithdrawCommand, and the deposit path does the same), so any player who can run the command can stall the server.

title: Bank.accrueInterest advances the clock when interest rounds to 0.00, losing it for good
fix: Only advance lastInterestAt when Currency.of(actual) is non-zero (or carry the fractional remainder), and return the rounded amount actually deposited
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] Interest is computed as a double, `double interest = balance * ratePerDay * elapsedDays;`, then deposited through `economy.depositAmount(Currency.of(actual))`, which rounds HALF_UP to cents, and `lastInterestAt = now;` runs regardless. Gangland's GanglandBankerEconomy.maintain calls accrueInterest on every banker interaction (documented as safe to call every interaction), so a 1000 balance at 1%/day accrues 0.00023 per interaction two seconds apart, which rounds to 0.00 while the elapsed time is consumed: active players never earn interest. In the opposite band, where each call's interest lands between 0.005 and 0.01, HALF_UP credits 0.01 each time and creates money. The method also returns the unrounded `actual`, so the caller reports interest that differs from what was credited.

title: PapiExpansionAdapter has no getRequiredPlugin, so PAPI keeps it after the owner disables
fix: Store the plugin name and override getRequiredPlugin() to return it (PAPI then unregisters it on PluginDisableEvent)
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] The adapter overrides getIdentifier/getAuthor/getVersion and `public boolean persist() { return true; }` but not getRequiredPlugin(), so it inherits null. PlaceholderAPI's LocalExpansionManager.onPluginDisable (verified in the 2.11.3 bytecode) unregisters an expansion only when `expansion.getRequiredPlugin()` equalsIgnoreCase the disabling plugin's name, and because the adapter class is loaded by Keystone's classloader, nothing else ties it to the consumer. Gangland registers `new PapiExpansionAdapter(this, FULL_PREFIX, placeholder)` and never unregisters it, so after Gangland disables (a failed enable or a plugin-manager reload), `%gangland_*%` keeps routing into the dead plugin's delegate and pins its classloader.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: ResourcePackTracker.active is one process-wide static, so each consumer installing a tracker clobbers the others
fix: Reject or warn on a second install, or scope the tracker per owning plugin rather than per JVM
observation: The tracker holds genuinely per-plugin state — `private final Set<UUID> loaded = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();`, the players who accepted *that* plugin's resource pack — behind a JVM-wide latch: `private static volatile ResourcePackTracker active;` with `public static void install(@Nullable ResourcePackTracker tracker) { active = tracker; }`. Keystone is loaded once and shared, so on a server running Gangland alongside Bartizan or Oriel the second plugin to install silently replaces the first, and every later `active()` lookup answers the wrong plugin's pack state. This is the same forbidden shape as the Diagnostics hub filed under DG, in a different class with a different fix site; the consequence here is pack-gated sounds or assets being enabled or suppressed for the wrong players.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: PdcPlayerMetaService silently drops set() and remove() for offline players
fix: Return a boolean or Result so callers learn the write was refused, or persist offline writes through the OfflinePlayer PDC
observation: set() resolves the player and abandons the write when they are not online: `Player online = Bukkit.getPlayer(player); if (online == null) { return; }` — no exception, no log, no return value, and remove() repeats it. The interface it implements is also satisfied by InMemoryPlayerMetaService, which stores the value regardless of online state, so the two implementations of one contract disagree about whether an offline write happens at all. A consumer writing player metadata during quit handling or from an async task that lands a tick late therefore loses the value silently, and the same call would have succeeded against the in-memory implementation used in its tests.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: Tree.size(), getAllNodes() and clone() throw NullPointerException once clear() has nulled the root
fix: Guard the root-walking methods for a null root and return 0 / an empty list
observation: clear() sets `this.root = null;`, but the traversal entry points do not check for it: `size()` is `return getNumberOfDescendants(root) + 1;` and getNumberOfDescendants immediately dereferences with `int size = root.getChildren().size();`. Any call to size(), getAllNodes() or clone() after a clear — or on a Tree that was never populated — throws NPE instead of reporting an empty tree. Tree is the structure backing the whole command argument system, so this sits underneath command registration rather than in an isolated helper.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: JsonFormatter.formatToJson mis-scopes its brace handling through operator precedence, corrupting quoted braces
fix: Parenthesise the conditions as `(c == '{' || c == '[') && !hasQuotes`
observation: The branches read `} else if (c == '{' || c == '[' && !hasQuotes) {` and `} else if (c == '}' || c == ']' && !hasQuotes) {`, and `&&` binds tighter than `||`, so each parses as `c == '{' || (c == '[' && !hasQuotes)`. The quote guard therefore applies only to brackets, never to braces: a `{` or `}` appearing inside a quoted string value still increments or decrements the indent level and injects a newline mid-string. Any JSON payload with a brace inside a quoted value comes out reindented and structurally mangled, and the sibling `:` and `,` branches show the guard was meant to apply to all of them.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: ScientificCalculator registers its custom operator and functions only when a non-empty variables map is supplied
fix: Register operators() and functions() on the builder unconditionally, and apply variables separately
observation: The constructor folds three unrelated concerns into one condition: `if (!(variables == null || variables.isEmpty())) builder.variables(variables.keySet()).operator(operators()).functions(functions());`. The custom factorial operator and the logb/neg/ln functions therefore exist only for expressions that also happen to declare variables, so a variable-free formula like `5!` or `ln(2)` is built without them and exp4j fails to resolve the token. The single-argument constructor below routes to exactly this path, so the simplest usage is the one that loses the features.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: LinkedList.clone() returns a shallow copy that shares the original's Node chain
fix: Deep-copy the node chain in clone() so the copy is independent
observation: clone() delegates straight to Object's shallow copy: `return (LinkedList<E>) super.clone();`. That copies the head and tail references rather than the nodes behind them, so the clone and the original share one chain — adding to or removing from either is visible in the other, and the size fields then disagree with the shared structure. A caller cloning a list precisely to mutate it without disturbing the original gets the opposite of what the method name promises, with no error to signal it.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: DurationParser.parse throws ArithmeticException on an overflowing duration instead of returning null like every other rejection
fix: Catch the overflow and return null, matching the method's existing contract for unparseable input
observation: Every other rejection path in parse returns null, but the unit conversion is unguarded: `case 'd' -> Duration.ofDays(amount);` and its siblings multiply into seconds with exact arithmetic, so a large admin-supplied value such as `999999999999d` raises an ArithmeticException that escapes the parser. A caller written against the documented null-on-failure contract has no catch for it, so a config typo becomes an exception on the config-load path rather than a rejected value.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: NumberUtil.resizeLinear divides by zero when the target size is 1, silently yielding 0
fix: Special-case targetSize == 1 (take the first or mean value) before the interpolation loop
observation: The interpolation maps indices with `double position = (double) i * (originalSize - 1) / (targetSize - 1);`, so a targetSize of 1 divides by zero. In double arithmetic that yields NaN for the i=0 case rather than throwing, and NaN then flows through `Math.floor` and the fraction into `Math.round`, which returns 0 — so shrinking a populated list to a single element silently produces a 0 instead of a representative value. The caller gets a plausible-looking result with no error, which is the failure mode hardest to notice downstream.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: PermissionWorker.permissionRefactor tests startsWith with no dot boundary, so a same-prefixed permission escapes canonicalisation
fix: Compare against `indicator + "."` (or check the first segment) rather than a bare startsWith
observation: Canonicalisation is decided by a bare prefix test: `return (!permission.startsWith(this.indicator) ? this.indicator + "." : "") + permission;`. With an indicator of `gang`, a permission such as `gangster.teleport` already "starts with" it, so the node is returned unprefixed and is registered and checked in a foreign namespace instead of `gang.gangster.teleport`. The mismatch is silent and self-consistent within one plugin only by luck — the same string can canonicalise differently depending on an unrelated plugin's naming. Note: the raw scanner cited lines 186-192, which do not exist in this 66-line file; the defect is real and verified at line 30.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: ActionBarManager's static per-player maps never evict entries for players who disconnect
fix: Remove a player's entries on quit, or sweep entries whose timestamps are long expired
observation: The arbitration state lives in two class-level maps, `private static final Map<UUID, Long> foregroundUntil = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();` and `private static final Map<UUID, BackgroundSlot> backgroundSlot = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();`, and every send path only ever puts into them. Nothing removes a UUID when the player leaves, so both grow by one entry per distinct player for the life of the server. The entries are small, so this is a slow leak rather than an urgent one; the statics themselves are arguably deliberate, since cross-plugin arbitration of a single action-bar slot only works if the state is shared.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: StaticResets omits EconomyHandler.vaultEconomy and CommandManager.commands, so consumer tests hand-roll their own resets
fix: Add reset helpers for the remaining process-wide statics the repo's testing conventions enumerate
observation: The class documents its own coverage as "the NmsVersion detection latch ..., the NbtBridge and PacketBridge seams", and the code matches — resetNmsVersion, resetNbtBridge, resetPacketBridge and nothing else. The repo's testing conventions name a longer list of process-wide statics that suites must reset, including `EconomyHandler.vaultEconomy` and `CommandManager.commands`, and the hooks tests already prove the need by implementing their own saveStatic/restoreStatic for the economy field. A consumer that trusts StaticResets to cover the documented set gets cross-test contamination from the two it silently does not handle.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: ChatUtil.capitalize throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException on an empty string
fix: Return the input unchanged when it is empty
observation: The helper is a bare two-substring expression with no length check: `return text.substring(0, 1).toUpperCase() + text.substring(1);`. An empty string — an unset config value, a blank display name, an empty enum label — makes `substring(0, 1)` throw. The parameter is annotated `@NotNull` so null is handled by contract, but emptiness is not, and the sibling `center` two lines below does validate its input via Preconditions.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: SpellChecker's optimised Damerau-Levenshtein transposition step computes the wrong distance
fix: Correct the transposition index arithmetic against the reference algorithm, and pin it with a test
observation: The reduced-memory Damerau-Levenshtein implementation mishandles the transposition case, so distances involving swapped adjacent characters come out higher than they should. The only consumer is the did-you-mean suggestion path behind an unknown command, so the visible effect is that a transposed typo may not surface the command the user meant, or ranks below a worse candidate. Suggestion quality only — no incorrect command ever executes — which is why this is P3 despite being a genuine algorithmic defect.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: ReflectionUtil.newInstance throws NullPointerException when any constructor argument is null
fix: Track the declared parameter types instead of deriving them from the argument instances
observation: The helper derives its parameter types from the supplied values, so a null argument has no class to read and the lookup NPEs before reflection is even attempted. That makes it impossible to construct an object through this helper with a legitimately null argument, which is an ordinary thing to want. A caller-supplied null is the only trigger and no current call site passes one, so it is a usability trap rather than a live fault.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: DbFiles.release relies on a one-second retry loop for Windows SQLite cleanup, the strategy this ecosystem documents as insufficient
fix: Close the pool's handles deterministically before deleting, keeping the retry only as a backstop
observation: release walks the directory deleting `.db`, `-wal` and `-shm` files and, on failure, sleeps and retries — "retrying up to 20 times with 50 ms pauses" per its own javadoc, a one-second total budget. The consuming project's documented lesson is the opposite: Windows file locks from HikariCP's eagerly-opened handles can persist for several seconds and retry loops alone are not a sufficient cleanup strategy. So the shared fixture bakes in the approach the ecosystem already learned does not hold, and consumer suites inherit flaky temp-directory cleanup. Test infrastructure only, never shipped, hence P3.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: Color enum maps two pairs of constants to the same chat code, leaving two legacy codes unreachable
fix: Give BROWN/ORANGE and PURPLE/MAGENTA distinct codes so all sixteen legacy colours are addressable
observation: Two pairs collide: `BROWN("&6", ...)` and `ORANGE("&6", ...)` share `&6`, and `PURPLE("&5", ...)` and `MAGENTA("&5", ...)` share `&5`. The sixteen constants therefore cover only fourteen distinct codes, and `&9` and `&c` are unreachable through this enum entirely. A consumer selecting BROWN and ORANGE gets identical output, and any reverse lookup from code to constant is ambiguous for the two duplicated codes.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: ServerEnvironment javadoc names the consumer plugin Oriel inside shared infrastructure
fix: Reword the javadoc in neutral terms
observation: The javadoc refers to Oriel by name in a keystone-common utility, breaking the hard rule that Keystone must not know its consumers. Comments only, so no behaviour is affected; it is the same class of drift filed for the diagnostics and placeholder packages under DG and PH, listed separately here because it is a different file with a different owner.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: NumberUtil.formatDouble's zero-strip regex corrupts non-English and no-decimal output
fix: Format with an explicit Locale (Locale.ROOT or a caller-supplied one) and strip zeros only after a decimal separator, e.g. via BigDecimal.stripTrailingZeros
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] formatDouble is `String.format(format, value).replaceAll("\\.?0*$", "")`, and valueFormat runs every value through it. String.format uses the JVM default locale, so on a German or French locale host `%,.2f` of 10 renders as `10,00` and the regex strips only the zeros, leaving `10,` (verified: 10 -> `10,`, 100 -> `100,`, -2500 -> `-2.500,`). With a caller format that has no decimal point, the regex eats trailing zeros from the integer part: `valueFormat("%.0f", 500)` returns `5`. Gangland feeds gang balances, bounties and experience into NumberUtil.valueFormat for its placeholders, so the displayed amounts are wrong on those hosts.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: NumberUtil.valueFormat(double) skips negatives and renders 999999 as 1,000K
fix: Scale on Math.abs(value) and re-apply the sign as the BigDecimal overload does, and re-check the suffix after rounding
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] The loop is `while (modValue >= 1_000 && index < SUFFIXES.length - 1)`, so any negative balance skips it and prints in full (-5000000 renders -5,000,000 while 5000000 renders 5M), unlike the BigDecimal overload, which handles `negative` explicitly. Rounding happens after the suffix is chosen, so 999999 becomes 999.999, formats as `1,000.00` and renders `1,000K` instead of `1M`. Cosmetic, but these strings reach player-facing placeholders.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: PermissionManager.removePermission skips permissionRefactor, so it removes nothing
fix: Canonicalise through permissionHandler.permissionRefactor(permission) before both the handler call and permissions.remove
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] addPermission stores the canonical form `permissions.add(permissionHandler.permissionRefactor(permission));` and PermissionWorker.addPermission registers `new Permission(permissionRefactor(permission))`, so `addPermission("update.check")` becomes `<prefix>.update.check`. removePermission passes the raw string through: PermissionWorker.removePermission throws `IllegalAccessException("Not allowed to access other plugins registered permission.")` because `update.check` does not start with the indicator (logged as a warning), and `permissions.remove(permission)` removes a string that was never in the set. The Bukkit Permission and the tracked entry both survive, and nothing tests removePermission.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: ParticleUtil ships product effects (jetpack, car exhaust, flashbang) inside Keystone
fix: Move the product-named effects to the consumer (Gangland or Bartizan) and keep only the generic primitives (spawnLine, cone, ring, burst) in keystone-common
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] CLAUDE.md's layering rule says a class that knows about weapons or any product concept does not belong in Keystone, yet ParticleUtil exposes `spawnJetpackFlame(Player player)` (L245), `spawnJetpackGlide` (L296), `spawnBurnoutSmoke(Location vehicleLocation, float yaw)` (L336), `spawnCarExhaust(..., boolean leftNozzle, boolean rightNozzle)` (L369), `spawnFlashbangBurst` (L400) and the deprecated `createBloodSplash(Entity entity, double damage)` (L557). These are Gangland/Bartizan vehicle, gadget and weapon visuals, not generic infrastructure. The conventions sweep matched only consumer symbols, not product vocabulary, so it did not catch these.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: LinkedList.removeAllOccurrences loops forever on the first match because current is never advanced after the unlink
fix: Capture next before unlinking and advance current = next in the match branch
observation: [found 2026-09-24 by the UC fixer, verified by the orchestrator] The loop only advances in the else branch: `if (current.data.equals(data)) { ... size--; } else current = current.next;`. When current matches, it is unlinked from its neighbours but current itself still points at the same node whose data still equals the argument, so the loop re-enters the match branch forever, decrementing size into negatives and re-unlinking. Any call with a value that is present hangs the calling thread (the main thread in a plugin), i.e. a server freeze.

sysName: Keystone · Utilities, data structures & test fixtures
title: StaticResets.resetAll throws NoClassDefFoundError for log4j on the testkit's own test classpath
fix: Add log4j-api/log4j-core to keystone-testkit at test scope only
observation: [found 2026-09-24 by the UC fixer] Some reset in StaticResets.resetAll touches the Keystone Logger, which needs log4j; keystone-testkit's own test classpath had none, so `resetAll()` threw `NoClassDefFoundError: org/apache/logging/log4j/LogManager` there and the testkit could not test its main entry point. Consumer classpaths carrying log4j were unaffected.

title: Timer.start after stop throws IllegalStateException because BukkitRunnable can only be scheduled once
fix: Stop extending BukkitRunnable and schedule a separate Runnable per start, so a Timer instance can be restarted
observation: Timer extends BukkitRunnable and start() schedules the instance itself: `if (async) this.bukkitTask = runTaskTimerAsynchronously(plugin, delay, period); else this.bukkitTask = runTaskTimer(plugin, delay, period);`. stop() then does `this.bukkitTask.cancel(); this.stopped.set(true); this.bukkitTask = null;`, which clears Keystone's own guard so a later start() proceeds — but Bukkit's BukkitRunnable.cancel() is only `Bukkit.getScheduler().cancelTask(getTaskId())` and never clears its internal task field, so the next schedule hits `checkNotYetScheduled()` and throws `IllegalStateException("Already scheduled as " + task.getTaskId())` (verified against the Spigot 1.16.5 API sources). Any stop-then-start on the same Timer, RepeatingTimer, CountdownTimer, CountupTimer or SequenceTimer therefore crashes, which is exactly what a managed reload does when it cancels timers and starts them again. Every existing timer test drives run() directly against a mocked isRunning() and never touches the real scheduler, so nothing catches it.

title: InMemoryCooldownService and PersistentCooldownService never evict entries for players who leave
fix: Evict a player's map on quit (or sweep expired entries periodically) instead of only on a repeat lookup of the same id
observation: The backing maps are `ConcurrentHashMap<UUID, Map<String, Long>>` and the only removal is lazy, inside the lookup for that exact key: `if (expiry <= System.currentTimeMillis()) { byId.remove(id); return 0L; }`. A player who triggers a cooldown once and then logs out is never queried again, so their UUID and its inner map stay resident for the life of the server. On a busy server with a rotating player base this grows without bound, and the persistent subclass keeps the same shape in its cache, so the leak is in both implementations.

title: PersistentCooldownService performs its schema, purge and upsert JDBC calls synchronously on the calling thread
fix: Move the persistence writes off the caller's thread (async task or write queue), keeping the in-memory update synchronous
observation: start() calls ensureReady() — which on first use runs backend.applySchema(...), a DELETE purge and a full-table SELECT — and then persistStart(), an upsert, all inline on whatever thread called CooldownService.start(). Cooldowns are set from gameplay paths (a click, a command, an ability), which run on the main server thread, so every cooldown write blocks the tick for a database round trip and the very first one blocks for a schema apply plus a full table read. On MySQL over a network that is a visible stall on a normal path; the in-memory sibling has no such cost, so a consumer swapping implementations silently inherits main-thread I/O.

title: PersistentCooldownService swallows every SQLException with a log.warn and continues as if persisted
fix: Report through Diagnostics and surface the degraded state rather than continuing silently
observation: ensureReady() ends with `catch (SQLException exception) { log.warn("Failed to initialise persistent cooldown store: {}", exception.toString(), exception); }` and persistStart() (lines 217-219) and persistClear() (lines 236-238) repeat the pattern, each continuing normally afterwards. The whole point of this implementation over the in-memory one is that cooldowns survive a restart, so a failing write means the persistence guarantee is quietly gone while the service reports success to its caller. The admin gets one warn line per failure and no fault in the diagnostics report, which is the log-and-swallow shape the repo's error rule forbids on a data path.

title: ClickDebounce keys every call site under one shared CLICK_DELAY_ID, so one site's delay overrides another's
fix: Include the call site (or an explicit id parameter) in the cooldown key instead of a single constant
observation: shouldSwallow takes a per-call `delayMillis` but always stores and reads the cooldown under the single constant CLICK_DELAY_ID. Two unrelated consumers of the same CooldownService — a GUI click handler on 200ms and an NPC interaction handler on 800ms — therefore share one debounce slot per player, so whichever fires first sets the window and the other is swallowed for a duration it never asked for. The per-call parameter reads like it scopes the debounce when it does not, making the wrong behaviour easy to miss.

title: SequenceTimer mutates its ArrayList and LinkedList queue with no synchronization against an async run()
fix: Use thread-safe collections or synchronize the queue mutations against run()
observation: addIntervalTaskPair() mutates intervalTaskPairs (ArrayList) and intervalTaskQueue (LinkedList), and reset() clears and repopulates the same LinkedList, while run() polls and mutates intervalTaskQueue on whichever thread the scheduler ticks it on. Started with start(true) the timer body runs on an async scheduler thread, so a consumer adding a pair or resetting from the main thread races the tick with no happens-before edge between them. The result is a lost or duplicated task step, or a LinkedList corrupted mid-traversal.

title: CooldownFormat.human renders Duration.ZERO as "1s" instead of an elapsed cooldown
fix: Return an empty or zero rendering for Duration.ZERO before applying the sub-second floor
tests: CooldownFormatTest (subSecondRoundsUpToOneSecond pins the floor that produces this)
observation: The formatter floors every duration with `long seconds = Math.max(duration.toSeconds(), 1);`, which is the intended rounding for a genuine sub-second remainder but also catches Duration.ZERO — the exact value CooldownService.remaining() returns by contract when a cooldown is not active. A player whose cooldown has elapsed is therefore shown "1s" remaining, and a consumer rendering remaining time unconditionally displays a cooldown that does not exist. CooldownFormatTest.subSecondRoundsUpToOneSecond pins the rounding rule, so fixing this means special-casing zero rather than changing the floor.

title: A null cooldown id throws NPE from the ConcurrentHashMap rather than failing gracefully
fix: Null-check the id at the service boundary and return not-active instead of propagating an NPE
observation: expiryOf() does `byId.get(id)` and start() does `expiries.computeIfAbsent(player, ...).put(id, expiry)` against ConcurrentHashMap, which rejects null keys with a NullPointerException where a plain HashMap would simply return null. A consumer resolving a cooldown id from config that turns out to be missing therefore gets an NPE out of a cooldown check rather than a clean miss. It takes a caller passing null, so this is a hardening gap at the boundary rather than an observed failure.

title: UpdateChecker.downloadLatestVersion keeps a truncated jar that then blocks every retry
fix: Download to a temp file with connect/read timeouts and atomically move it into place only after a complete transfer; delete the temp file on any exception
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] The download opens `ReadableByteChannel readableByteChannel = Channels.newChannel(url.openStream());` with no connect or read timeout (unlike getLatestVersion, which sets TIMEOUT_MS), then streams straight into the final file `new File(releaseFolder, plugin.getName() + "-" + latestVersion + ".jar")` via `fileOutputStream.getChannel().transferFrom(readableByteChannel, 0, Long.MAX_VALUE)`. If the connection drops or the async thread is interrupted mid-transfer, the catch only logs and the partial jar stays on disk. Every later call (the UpdateNotifier auto-update path runs it once per interval) then hits `if (outputFile.exists()) { log.info("Version {} is already downloaded at {}", ...); return false; }`, so the corrupt jar is reported as already downloaded forever and an admin who copies it from release/ installs a broken plugin. A stalled server with no read timeout can also pin the async worker indefinitely.

title: PersistentCooldownService.ensureReady retries schema apply, purge and full SELECT on every isActive/remaining call while it keeps failing
fix: Latch the failure (retry on a backoff or only from onInitialize) so the read path never re-enters JDBC
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] isActive and remaining both open with `ensureReady();`, and ensureReady returns early only `if (ready || !isConnected())`; `ready = true` is set only after applySchema, the DELETE purge and the full-table SELECT all succeed (lines 147-185), and the catch just logs. So with a connected backend whose initialisation keeps failing (a DDL permission error, an incompatible pre-existing table, a lock timeout), every cooldown read, the path the class javadoc says "never touch[es] the database", re-runs the whole schema apply + purge + table scan synchronously and logs a full stack trace. Cooldown checks sit on click/command/ability paths on the main thread, so a persistent init failure becomes per-interaction main-thread JDBC plus log flooding. Distinct from row 3 (first successful init and write-through on start()): this is the unbounded retry on the read path.

title: PersistentCooldownService's legacy-Database path shares the Database table cursor and connection without synchronizing on it
fix: Wrap the legacy-path calls in synchronized (database), as DatabaseHelper.runQueries does, or route them through a DatabaseHelper
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] The legacy Database is a stateful cursor: SQLite/MySQL.table(name) stores `this.table = tableName` and the following insert/delete/buildUpsertQuery read getTable(), all over one long-lived Connection. AbstractRepository's legacy saves hold `synchronized (database)` through DatabaseHelper.runQueries while calling `database.table(name)` and, in Table.batchUpsertTableQuery, `conn.setAutoCommit(false)` on that same connection; PersistentCooldownService calls `QueryBuilder.on(database, table).delete()...execute()` and `.insert()...execute()` (and ensureReady's createTable/delete/selectAll at lines 169-176) with no lock, from the main thread. When a cooldown starts during an async autosave the threads interleave table() and the statement, so either side's SQL is built against the other's table ("no such column", swallowed with a warn, and the save or the cooldown row is lost). A cooldown write issued mid-batch also joins the repository's open transaction and is rolled back with it if the batch fails. The trigger is the documented construction, passing handler.getDatabase().

title: Diagnostics.install unconditionally overwrites the process-wide active hub, so the last consumer to boot steals every plugin's fault sink
fix: Make install() reject or warn when a hub is already active, or key the active hub per owning plugin
tests: DiagnosticsTest (resets the static between tests rather than asserting install-collision behaviour)
observation: The installer is `public static void install(Diagnostics diagnostics) { active = diagnostics; }` — a bare assignment to one JVM-wide static with no already-installed check and no warning. Keystone is loaded once and shared, so on a server running Gangland plus Bartizan or Oriel the second plugin to bootstrap silently replaces the first plugin's hub, and every later `Diagnostics.active()` call from the first plugin routes its faults into the second plugin's sink and fault table. The repo's own shared-classloader rule names exactly this pattern — a static singleton holding per-plugin state — as forbidden, and the consequence is misattributed and misrouted diagnostics on precisely the multi-consumer servers this library exists to serve.

title: PlayerInputInterceptor.channelRead swallows every exception from apply() with an empty catch
fix: Report through Diagnostics (rate-limited) instead of an empty catch, so a broken subscriber is visible
observation: Every inbound player-input packet runs `try { apply(session, parsePacket(msg)); } catch (Exception ignored) { }` on the Netty IO thread. Any failure in a concrete subclass's apply() — a consumer's vehicle or jetpack input handling — or in parsePacket's reflection is discarded with no log, no fault and no counter, so the feature simply stops responding while the server looks healthy. This is the exact log-and-swallow shape the repo's Result/Diagnostics rule forbids, made worse by sitting on a per-packet hot path where an admin has no other signal.

title: PlayerInputInterceptor.ensureReflectionReady silently disables input parsing forever when the NMS packet class fails to resolve
fix: Report a fault when resolution fails so the degraded state is visible instead of silently permanent
observation: Resolution is one-shot and its failure path is silent: `try { resolveAgainst(Class.forName("net.minecraft.network.protocol.game.ServerboundPlayerInputPacket")); } catch (Exception ignored) { packetClass = null; } finally { reflectionReady = true; }`. Setting reflectionReady in the finally means the failure is cached permanently for the JVM, and channelRead's guard `if (reflectionReady && packetClass != null && ...)` then skips every packet for the rest of the server's uptime. On a Minecraft build that renames the packet class or its accessors, every consumer's input-driven feature goes dead at once with not a single line in the console explaining why.

title: ReflectivePacketAdapter.updateTitleThroughPackets lets NmsCache wiring failure escape as an uncaught IllegalStateException
fix: Catch IllegalStateException alongside ReflectiveOperationException and degrade to the non-packet path
observation: The pre-1.20 title fallback calls `NmsCache cache = NmsCache.get();` inside a block guarded only by `catch (ReflectiveOperationException ex)`. NmsCache.build() wraps any reflective wiring failure in an IllegalStateException, which is unchecked and therefore sails straight through that catch to the caller. On a server in the supported 1.16.5-to-1.19 range where the reflective handles fail to wire, a routine title update throws instead of degrading, surfacing as a stack trace on whatever consumer path requested it. The adapter's whole purpose is to degrade rather than throw, so the narrow catch defeats its own contract.

title: PlayerInputInterceptor offers no shared unregister path, leaving Netty handler removal to each of three consumers
fix: Ship a static uninstall(player)/uninstallAll() helper beside the documented install snippet
observation: The class javadoc hands the caller both halves of the lifecycle as raw pipeline calls — install with `pipeline().addBefore("packet_handler", HANDLER_NAME, handler)` and remove it with `pipeline().remove(HANDLER_NAME)` — while owning all the reflection and version guards itself. Removal on quit and on plugin disable is therefore reimplemented independently by every consumer, and a consumer that misses either case leaks the handler and the Player reference it closes over for the rest of uptime, with a duplicate handler installed on rejoin. No leak exists inside Keystone itself, so this is an API-hardening gap rather than a live fault, but it is a sharp edge on a class three plugins subclass.

title: DefaultClassifiers.byOriginatingPackage classifies genuine bugs inside Keystone's own nms package as DEPENDENCY
fix: Drop org.luckyraven.keystone.nms from DEPENDENCY_PACKAGES, or match only genuinely third-party frames
observation: DEPENDENCY_PACKAGES contains both `"me.clip.placeholderapi"` and `"org.luckyraven.keystone.nms"`, and the rule matches when either the fault's class name or `stack[0].getClassName()` starts with one of them. The first entry is a genuine third party; the second is Keystone's own code, so an internal defect in the NMS layer is reported to admins as someone else's dependency problem rather than as a Keystone bug. That misdirects triage for exactly the reflection-heavy area most likely to break on a server upgrade.

title: LanguageLoader.tryLoadFromDisk degrades to jar defaults through a console-only log.warn, never through Diagnostics
fix: Route the IOException through Diagnostics/Fault so the silent fallback to bundled defaults is a reportable event
observation: The disk-load failure path catches IOException from the FileHandler pipeline with only `log.warn("FileHandler error for {}.yml: {}", fileName, exception.getMessage());` and returns null, which sends loadMessage() quietly back to the bundled jar resource. An admin whose translated language file is unreadable or malformed therefore sees their customised strings silently replaced by shipped defaults, with a single warn line and nothing in the fault report. It is the log-and-swallow pattern the repo's own error rule forbids, on the path that decides what every player reads.

title: Keystone javadoc names consumer products (Oriel, Gangland, Bartizan) across six files
fix: Rewrite the affected javadoc in neutral terms (the consumer, the host plugin)
observation: Diagnostics.java:11 states "Every classified failure in Oriel flows through here exactly once", DefaultClassifiers.java:13 says "The rules encode Oriel's house conventions", and FaultKind.java:12,23,28 describe faults as "written to the oriel_faults table" and "Oriel caused this... not a bug in Oriel". The hard layering rule is that Keystone must not know its consumers; these are comments rather than code, so nothing misbehaves, but they misinform the other two consumers reading the same API and describe a fault table name that does not match what a Gangland or Bartizan server actually writes to.

title: PlayerInputInterceptor binds only Mojang names, so it is dead below Paper 1.21.2
fix: Resolve the channel through NmsCache's multi-name connection lookup and add the Spigot packet names (PacketPlayInSteerVehicle) and the getXxa/getZza/isJumping/isShiftKeyDown accessors
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] getChannel walks only Mojang field names: `Object packetListener = getField(serverPlayer, "connection");` then `getField(packetListener, "connection")`; on Spigot 1.16.5 the fields are playerConnection/networkManager (and obfuscated b/c on Spigot 1.17+), so it returns null. ensureReflectionReady loads only `Class.forName("net.minecraft.network.protocol.game.ServerboundPlayerInputPacket")`, a Mojang name that does not exist on any Spigot runtime, and its pre-1.21.2 branch asks for `packet.getMethod("xxa")` / `zza` / `jumping`, while the real pre-1.21.2 Mojang packet exposes getXxa()/getZza()/isJumping()/isShiftKeyDown(), so that branch cannot bind on any real server either. The class javadoc advertises pre-1.21.2 support and Keystone's floor is Spigot 1.16.5, yet the only runtime where input parsing works is Mojang-mapped Paper 1.21.2+. NmsCache already solves the connection lookup with `firstField(entityPlayerClass, "playerConnection", "connection", "c", "b")`. Distinct from #3 (which is about the silent failure, not the unreachable bindings); the green test only binds synthetic fixture classes named after the assumed accessors.

title: CameraRotationPackets omits DELTA flags, so on 1.21.2+ each recoil zeroes player velocity
fix: On the PositionMoveRotation shape add the Relative DELTA_X, DELTA_Y, DELTA_Z (and ROTATE_DELTA) constants to the flag set so the client keeps its momentum
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] relativeFlags always picks `String[] wanted = {"X", "Y", "Z", "Y_ROT", "X_ROT"};` and the modern shape builds `moveCtor.newInstance(zero, zero, deltaYaw, deltaPitch)` with a Vec3.ZERO delta movement. From 1.21.2 the client computes the new velocity as the packet's delta movement plus the current velocity only for axes flagged DELTA_X/DELTA_Y/DELTA_Z, so with those flags absent it sets the player's velocity to zero on every packet (pre-1.21.2 the X/Y/Z relative flags alone preserved momentum, which is why the legacy shapes were fine). ReflectivePacketAdapter.relativeCameraRotation is the recoil path Bartizan installs, so on 1.21.2+ every shot stops a sprinting, strafing or falling shooter mid-motion. CameraRotationPacketsTest deliberately pins that DELTA_X and ROTATE_DELTA are excluded, which proves the flag selection, not the client-side effect.

title: PacketBridge.reset() from one disabling consumer turns off every consumer's packets
fix: Reference-count installs per owning plugin (install(plugin, adapter) / release(plugin)) or make reset() a no-op while other owners remain
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] The adapter lives in `private static volatile PacketAdapter adapter = NoOpAdapter.INSTANCE;` and `reset()` unconditionally sets `PacketBridge.adapter = NoOpAdapter.INSTANCE;`. Oriel (AnimationConfig) and Bartizan (KernelConfig) each call `PacketBridge.install(adapter)` at bootstrap, and Bartizan's KernelConfig documents that `Bartizan.onDisable()` calls `PacketBridge.reset()`. When Bartizan is disabled at runtime (a failed enable, a plugin-manager reload) while Oriel keeps running, Oriel's inventory-title animation, furnace fake windows and property updates silently route to the no-op adapter for the rest of uptime with nothing logged. This is the same shared-classloader last-writer shape as Diagnostics.install (#1), but on a separate static that no existing row covers.

title: DefaultPlaceholderProvider reads world and chunk state with no documented main-thread contract
fix: Document the provider as main-thread-only and resolve %biome% from a cached value, or guard the chunk-loading reads
observation: resolve() reaches into live world state for several tokens, the sharpest being `s = replace(s, "%biome%", () -> online.getLocation().getBlock().getBiome().name());` — getBlock() touches the chunk and can trigger a chunk load — alongside `online.getWorld().getName()`, the location reads and `Bukkit.getOnlinePlayers().size()`. Placeholder resolution is exactly the kind of text rendering consumers commonly drive from async scoreboard or timer tasks, and neither this class nor the PlaceholderProvider interface states a threading requirement anywhere. No async caller exists inside Keystone today, so this is filed as a latent trap rather than a proven main-thread violation — but it becomes a P0 the moment any of the three consumers renders a board off-thread, and nothing in the API warns them.

title: CompositePlaceholderProvider.resolve isolates nothing, so one throwing provider breaks the whole chain
fix: Wrap each provider call in try/catch that reports through Diagnostics and passes the previous value through
observation: The chain is a bare loop: `for (PlaceholderProvider provider : providers) { value = provider.resolve(player, value); }`. The PlaceholderProvider contract does say implementations should never throw, but this class exists precisely to chain providers it does not control — including ones registered by a consumer plugin — so a single misbehaving provider propagates its exception out of the whole resolve call and takes down the chat message, scoreboard line or GUI title being rendered. The repo's own house pattern elsewhere (VaultOfflinePermissionService) is to catch, report and degrade, which is what the composite should do here.

title: PlaceholderHandler inherits PlaceholderRequest.onRequest returning null, so direct use silently resolves nothing
fix: Make PlaceholderHandler abstract on onRequest so a subclass must supply it, instead of inheriting a null-returning default
observation: PlaceholderHandler extends PlaceholderRequest but declares no onRequest override, so it inherits the base implementation's `return null;`. CharReplacer.apply treats a null result as unresolved and reconstructs the original `%token%` text verbatim, so a consumer instantiating PlaceholderHandler directly — which its public constructor invites — gets a handler that quietly resolves nothing and leaves raw tokens in player-facing text. There is no compile-time signal and no runtime warning that the class must be subclassed to do anything.

title: Built-in placeholder providers NPE on a null OfflinePlayer that the sibling effect SPI accepts
fix: Null-check player at the top of each provider's resolve and skip the player-scoped tokens
observation: CooldownPlaceholderProvider dereferences the player unconditionally once its quick contains-check passes (`UUID uuid = player.getUniqueId();`), and MetaPlaceholderProvider plus DefaultPlaceholderProvider have the same gap (`player.getName()` at DefaultPlaceholderProvider.java:56). The placeholder effect SPI alongside them explicitly supports a null player for server-scoped text, so the two halves of the same subsystem disagree on whether null is legal. A consumer rendering server-wide text with no player context therefore gets an NPE out of a provider rather than the server-scoped tokens it expected.

title: The flash placeholder effect layer is fully built and tested but wired to nothing, and holds classloader-wide static state
fix: Decide it: either wire the effect layer into CharReplacer/PlaceholderHandler and namespace its static state per plugin, or delete it
observation: A repo-wide grep for processFlash, processConditionalFlash, isFlashPlaceholder, FlashEffect and FlashPlaceholderWrapper outside the effect package and its own tests returns zero hits — nothing in PlaceholderHandler, CharReplacer, PlaceholderProvider or CompositePlaceholderProvider ever calls into it, so no consumer's `%flash...%` token can ever resolve despite the feature being documented, implemented and unit-tested. It also carries state that would breach the shared-classloader rule the moment it were wired: `private static final Map<String, FlashState> flashStates = new HashMap<>();` keyed on raw placeholder text with no per-plugin namespace, plus a JVM-wide `@Setter private static long currentTick`. The two halves are one decision, so they are filed together rather than as separate findings.

title: PlaceholderHandler recompiles its Pattern and format string on every call
fix: Hoist the compiled Pattern into a static final field and precompute the prefix format per instance
observation: containsPlaceholder builds a fresh matcher each time with `Pattern.compile(PLACEHOLDER_PATTERN).matcher(text).find()` even though PLACEHOLDER_PATTERN is a static final constant, and replacePlaceholder recomputes `String.format("%%%s_", prefix)` although prefix is fixed per instance. Placeholder resolution runs per line per player per scoreboard tick, so this recompiles a regex thousands of times a second on a populated server. Pure waste rather than incorrect output, hence P3.

title: Placeholder effect javadoc names Gangland domain concepts (wanted level, gang bounty, GTA-style)
fix: Rewrite the examples with neutral placeholder names
observation: The class javadoc teaches the feature with `%flashif:user_wanted>0:5:5:user_wanted%` and `%flashif:gang_bounty>0:user_bounty%`, and FlashEffect.java:9 describes the whole thing as "a GTA-style flash effect". Wanted levels and gang bounties are Gangland Warfare's own domain entities, so shared infrastructure is documenting itself in one consumer's vocabulary — the same layering rule broken by the diagnostics javadoc filed under DG, but in different files with a different owner. Comments only, so nothing misbehaves; it misleads the other two consumers reading the same API.

title: ConditionalFlashWrapper's pattern never matches >= or <=, so those conditions are false
fix: Order the alternation longest-first (>=|<=|==|!=|>|<) and make the left operand reluctant
observation: [found 2026-09-24, master 4192baa] The pattern is `Pattern.compile("flashif:([^:]+)(>|<|>=|<=|==|!=)([^:]+)(?::(\\d+):(\\d+))?:(.+)")`. Because `>` and `<` come before `>=` and `<=` in the alternation, `flashif:%level%>=5:%x%` matches as operator `>` with right operand `=5` (verified with the same regex: groups ('%level%', '>', '=5', ...)). evaluateCondition then fails `parseNumber("=5")` and falls to the string branch, where `default -> false` makes every >= and <= condition false, so the flash never fires. No test covers ConditionalFlashWrapper. The layer is currently unwired (#5), so this is a latent trap for the first consumer that adopts it.

title: FlashEffect divides by zero when a flash:0:0 placeholder is parsed from config
fix: Reject non-positive on/off durations in FlashPlaceholderWrapper.processFlash and fall back to the defaults
